items.body:
While it shows a decline in sales for Booker, reflecting the impact of lapping strong growth in the prior year and the continued decline of the tobacco market, a slight increase in operating profit was achieved via better buying terms and strong execution of Tesco’s ‘Save to Invest’ cost-efficiency program, effectively offsetting the drop in overall sales volumes
Booker’s total sales excluding tobacco was down 1.4%, while tobacco sales dropped 8.9% to £740m.
Traditional tobacco sales have been steadily declining due to regulatory changes, tax increases, and shifting consumer preferences toward vaping or quitting, while non-tobacco grocery categories continue to grow.
That is reflected throughout the sector with Tesco’s total convenience like-for-like sales (including One Stop stores) declining by 1.7% in the first half of fiscal year 2026, driven primarily by the continuing contraction in the tobacco market.
On a two-year basis, however, Booker, excluding tobacco, was up 2.7%.
Booker’s symbol brands (including Premier, Londis, Budgens, and Family Shopper) continued to deliver strong performance, supported by the addition of 275 net new retail partners during the period.
Despite lower overall volume, Tesco said the results demonstrate that Booker successfully managed its sales mix and operational costs to maintain a stable profit contribution to the Tesco Group.
Tesco Express sales were broadly flat year-on-year with performance supported by a 1.4 percentage points contribution from net new store openings.

items.body:
Datekin lands on Ocado.com, the world’s largest dedicated online supermarket, from 8th October, its first listing with a mainstream UK grocer, and the latest in a fast run of listings for the brand that launched in spring 2025.
Ocado Retail’s buying team has taken two lines: the Datekin Sukkari Pitted Dates Family Share Pack (12 x 30g, RRP £9.99) and Datekin Coconut & Tahini Date Balls (5-pack, RRP £2.49). Both launch on promotion at 33% off.
Ocado.com reaches over 80% of the UK population and serves more than 1 million active customers, with a range of around 50,000 products – putting Datekin in front of one of the largest online grocery audiences in the country.
The two lines going into Ocado.com are aimed at the household shop: twelve individually portioned 30g packs of soft, golden pitted Sukkari dates built for lunchboxes and packed lunches, and bite-sized pressed date balls with a roasted tahini centre rolled in desiccated coconut- both products are high in fibre, no added sugar, vegan and vegetarian.
The launch comes as new research* by the brand reveals a gap in Brits’ fibre knowledge. While one in three plan to eat more fibre in 2027, just 36% know how much they actually need. With adults advised to eat 30g a day, Datekin offers a simple way to boost fibre intake, with every product naturally high in fibre, making it an easy, everyday addition to the weekly shop.
Datekin launched in spring 2025 and has gone from a standing start to Selfridges, Amazon, more than 40 WHSmith Travel stores across the UK, and over 400 independent coffee shops and deli’s. In July, the brand picked up a one-star Great Taste award for its Date Filled Whole Wheat & Bran Cakes, and in September it won Best New Product for Food and Drink at the Glee trade show.
What sits behind the growth is owned supply and organic demand. Datekin’s dates are grown, handpicked and pitted on the founder’s family farms in Saudi Arabia – the brand’s direct supply chain is vital at a time when the wider category is wrestling with shortages and shipping costs. Increased organic demand from shoppers for a more natural snacking range has been apparent with shoppers looking for a clean and simple ingredients list, which Datekin can meet with the latest range going into Ocado only having 1 to 3 ingredients.
Megan Matthews, head of marketing at Datekin, said: “We’ve moved quickly since launching in spring 2025, and the reason we’ve been able to is that we own our farms and hold our stock here in the UK. That’s what lets us say yes to a retailer like Ocado. Their buyers can see the growth of the natural snacking category, and they’ve chosen to back both our Family Share Pack and our coconut date balls from day one – this is the listing that puts Datekin into the weekly online shop. ”
Lily Bentley, snacks & nuts buyer at Ocado.com, added: “I am excited to introduce Datekin to Ocado’s snack range, launching two of their products! Demand for high-fibre, whole-food options continues to grow, and Datekin’s products align well with what our customers are looking for – combining clean-label ingredients with functional health benefits.”

items.title: Amazon job cuts hit hundreds as tech giant denies AI link

The company confirmed on Wednesday that it was reducing headcount across its Stores division, which oversees its core online retail operations, with employees in the UK, US [...]
items.body:
Amazon job cuts hit hundreds as tech giant denies AI link
Amazon’s latest round of job cuts will affect hundreds of employees worldwide, City AM understands, as the tech giant continues to restructure its business following nearly 30,000 redundancies.
The company confirmed on Wednesday that it was reducing headcount across its Stores division, which oversees its core online retail operations, with employees in the UK, US and India among those affected.
While Amazon has not publicly disclosed the scale of the cuts, City AM understands the number of affected employees is in the hundreds, with only a handful impacted within its UK workforce.
The latest redundancies are also understood to be unrelated to AI, despite coming as Amazon invests heavily in the technology.
“We’re always looking at our team structures to ensure we’re best set up to move fast as we innovate for customers”, said an Amazon spokesperson.
“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities”.
The company said it had made the “difficult decision” to eliminate a small number of roles and would support affected employees through the transition.
The reductions follow two much larger rounds of redundancies, with Amazon cutting around 14,000 corporate jobs in late 2025 and another 16,000 in January.
Those cuts spanned several divisions, including Amazon Web Services, as the company sought to reduce management layers and simplify its operations.
Layoffs mount amid AI investment boom
Amazon’s latest restructuring comes as tech companies continue to cut jobs while pouring billions into AI and infrastructure.
Several major firms have announced substantial redundancies this year, although the extent to which AI is responsible varies.
Oracle said in a regulatory filing that adopting AI had contributed to workforce reductions, while Microsoft and Meta have also cut thousands of jobs as they increase investment in the technology.
Amazon has continued recruiting in specialist areas, including AI and machine learning, even as it reduces headcount elsewhere.
The company has reportedly approached former employees about returning to its cloud division, including some affected by previous restructuring rounds.
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos attributed the company’s earlier job cuts to excessive hiring during the pandemic, when a surge in online shopping prompted the business to expand rapidly.
As demand returned to normal, Amazon was left with a larger workforce than it needed, he said in an interview with Fox News.
The latest cuts also coincide with Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days shopping event, one of its biggest promotional periods of the year.
Amazon has maintained that its restructuring is intended to make the business faster and more efficient, rather than being driven by a single technology or a downturn in demand.

items.title: Tesco urges Healey to slash ‘fundamentally unfair’ business rates
items.summary: The boss of Tesco has urged John Healey to reform the “fundamentally unfair” business rates system and avoid a so-called warehouse tax.  Ken Murphy, chief executive of the UK’s biggest grocer, has become the latest retail industry figure to urge the Chancellor to cut taxes on high street businesses, as Andy Burnham pledges a revival [...]
items.body:
Tesco urges Healey to slash ‘fundamentally unfair’ business rates
The boss of Tesco has urged John Healey to reform the “fundamentally unfair” business rates system and avoid a so-called warehouse tax.
Ken Murphy, chief executive of the UK’s biggest grocer, has become the latest retail industry figure to urge the Chancellor to cut taxes on high street businesses, as Andy Burnham pledges a revival of the country’s town centres.
The Prime Minister has reportedly been considering hiking the highest business rates multiplier to pay for tax cuts for pubs and smaller shops, but retailers have warned higher taxes on warehouses would push up prices for shoppers.
Murphy told reporters on Thursday: “We have long argued that the rate system is fundamentally unfair, that retailers pay – on average – four times their fair share of rates.
“We have urged the government for a more equitable rates system. Our one ask of the government going into this budget is that they exempt all retail businesses from the half-a-million pound rateable value threshold.”
In recent months, retail bosses have been ramping up pressure on Labour to commit to its election manifesto pledge to “replace” the business rates system.
The British Retail Consortium (BRC) – which represents grocers like Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Marks & Spencer – has urged Healey to bring down the “punishing” tax burden facing the industry.
Retailers pay 72p in tax for every pound they make, according to the BRC’s analysis, which makes it the second-highest taxpaying sector, behind only hospitality.
Tesco vows to limit inflation
Tesco lifted its profit forecast on Thursday after seeing a boost in online sales, though its group like-for-like sales dipped from one per cent to 0.9 per cent growth in the second quarter.
Murphy said British shoppers are proving “resilient” despite warnings that food inflation could surge next year, due to rising energy and shipping costs caused by the Iran war.
In April, the Tesco boss said he did not recognise a forecast by the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), which claimed food inflation could reach 10 per cent by the end of this year.
The FDF now expects food inflation to peak at 6.4 per cent in July next year. Murphy said he “can’t predict too much,” adding that Tesco is committed to providing “the best possible value for customers”.
He said: “I’m particularly pleased with the fact that when people were talking about high inflation in April, we said we didn’t see it, that we felt that inflation on food was under control, and I think that’s proven to be true over the six months.
“[Food] inflation is now well below the rate of wage inflation. So I think that’s something to feel really good about.”
The Grocery Code Adjudicator, a government watchdog, is meeting with supermarkets in the coming weeks over concerns that grocers are refusing price increase requests from suppliers who have seen their costs surge.
Murphy said Tesco has been “very clear and consistent” that it will not accept price increases if they are “not justified” by suppliers.

items.title: Eighty one per cent expect to be better prepared for disruption but 54% still manage supply chain risk reactively, BSI finds

Organisations are increasingly confident they can withstand the next supply chain disruption, but many lack the processes, visibility and coordination needed to respond effectively when it happens, new research from BSI finds. While 81% expect to be better prepared for disruption over the next 12 months, more than half (54%) say their approach to supply […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Organisations are increasingly confident they can withstand the next supply chain disruption, but many lack the processes, visibility and coordination needed to respond effectively when it happens, new research from BSI finds.
While 81% expect to be better prepared for disruption over the next 12 months, more than half (54%) say their approach to supply chain risk management remains largely reactive. Just one in four (27%) can take action on the same day when disruption strikes, while 37% did not follow a crisis plan during their most recent disruption.
Drawing on a global study of more than 1,400 managers across supply chain, finance, procurement, operations and legal functions, the report Building for disruption: the new outlook for supply chain resilience, raises fears that the gap between intention and implementation could leave businesses exposed to shortages, delays and higher operating costs. With more than a third (36%) of organizations planning to increase prices over the next six months to offset supply chain costs, the consequences are likely to extend beyond business operations and be felt by consumers.
Over the past 12 months 40% have experienced climate-related disruptions, more than a third (38%) were impacted by cyber incidents, 38% having been affected by conflict, sanctions or political instability, 35% faced component or raw material shortages, and nearly four in 10 (39%) encountered transport disruptions.
A significant crisis readiness gap exists between intention and execution, with 45% of organizations planning to undertake cross-functional scenario planning, yet few carrying it out consistently. Even amongst those with an always-on crisis response team, activation can take up to three days (33%). The gap is highlighted by the finding that 37% did not follow their pre-agreed crisis plan during the recent Iran and Israel conflict.
Processes, visibility and silos are holding organizations back
The research suggests that shortcomings in processes, visibility and cross-functional coordination are preventing organizations from responding effectively to supply chain threats.
- 43% of organizations lack a formal, documented process for managing supply chain risks, and slow or unclear approval processes are preventing decisions being made for more than two in five (44%), while only four in 10 (39%) have clear protocols for cross-functional communication when disruptions arise.
- Effective decision-making is also being hampered by poor visibility, with 38% citing a lack of timely and accurate data as a barrier to responding quickly and confidently to supply chain threats. Just a third (33%) have complete visibility of supplier locations and geographic exposure.
- More than one-third (38%) say silos and poor cross functional coordination is a barrier to effective decision making, and 28% say they experience conflicting priorities between teams and departments. Only 4 in 10 (38%) say cross-functional teams meet regularly (at least weekly).
Managing the permacrisis and AI
Despite these gaps, organizations are beginning to rethink how they build resilience. Rather than focusing solely on recovering from the last disruption, many are making structural changes to how and where they source, store and move goods, reflecting a shift towards building long-term resilience in an increasingly volatile operating environment.
- Looking ahead to the next six months, organizations are actively altering their operations to build endurance:
- 80% plan to increase strategic inventory stockpiles
- 79% intend to change transport modes
- 78% are moving to nearshore key operations
- 33% are seeking new supplier networks
- 28% plan to reduce product ranges or SKUs
- 24% expect to shift trade routes entirely
However, despite these efforts, only 35% say they feel fully prepared for geopolitical shocks, while just 34% feel ready to manage raw material shortages and 37% cyber incidents.
The report also highlights additional emerging threats on the horizon. Two-thirds of respondents (59%) believe artificial intelligence will increase the risk of theft and cybercrime in supply chains, yet barely a third (34%) feel fully prepared to handle severe technology failures or cyber incidents. As digital dependencies grow alongside physical supply risks, BSI emphasizes that end-to-end network visibility will be vital for long-term organizational survival.
Tony Pelli, practice director, supply chain resilience, BSI, said: “2026 has been the hottest summer on record for several countries, and with conditions set to remain volatile into 2027 due to El Niño patterns, the human element of these disruptions is stark. A set of unrelenting environmental and geopolitical ruptures means that supply chain breakdown directly impacts everyday lives. When networks fail, people ultimately bear the burden through rising shelf prices and an inability to access the essential goods they rely on.”
David Fairnie, senior principal consultant, supply chain resilience, BSI, said: “The research shows that the majority of organisations expect to be well prepared for disruption over the next 12-months, yet they don’t have the foundations of resilience firmly in place. With more than half describing their approach to risk management as reactive, and a widespread lack of formal, documented processes for managing supply chain risk, there is an opportunity to embed best practice to enable proactive resilience.”
“Resilience means strengthening scenario planning, improving cross-functional coordination, increasing supply chain visibility, and ensuring leaders have the information they need to act quickly and confidently when disruption strikes.”

The midi skirt is having its moment this season, as the wear-with-everything length makes its way back to the forefront of our wardrobes.
From tailored styles to satin, lace, and checks, the midi is proving there’s no single way to wear the trend. Its appeal lies in that versatility, long enough to work with boots as temperatures drop, but easy to pair with trainers or loafers on milder autumn days.
Right now, it’s all about finding a midi with a little something extra, whether that’s an unexpected texture, print, or shape. Hush has plenty to choose from across different styles and colourways, including a gorgeous pinstripe version that puts a contemporary spin on the classic length.
This midi skirt combines a soft wool blend with a charcoal pinstripe, bringing a tailored feel to its asymmetric silhouette. Draping through the skirt creates movement at the hem, making it an easy way to bring a little more interest to simple autumn outfits.
Pair it with a T-shirt and trainers while the weather is still mild, then switch to an oversized knit and knee-high boots as temperatures drop. From workdays to weekends, it’s the kind of skirt that earns its place in the autumn rotation.

Findings from the US […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
American consumers are hungry for UK and European fashion, but brands are capturing only a fraction of the opportunity, says new research from SoldThrough – a fashion logistics and marketplace management company that helps international brands launch, expand and scale across American marketplace channels and retailers including Nordstrom, Bloomingdale’s and Macy’s.
Findings from the US consumer survey, released today, found that 81% say UK and European fashion brands offer something that US brands cannot match, from higher quality materials (25%) and better craftsmanship (24%), to better value for money (24%), greater longevity (14%) and heritage (12%) .
At the same time, more than half (57%) – equivalent to 157.7 million US adults – are already purchasing UK and European fashion, spending an average of $219.20 each a year, a figure that represents a $34.5bn annual market. The categories consumers most want to buy from UK and European brands are accessories (27%), followed by shoes (26%).
However, while demand is clear, for a significant proportion of the population, getting from interest to purchase is proving difficult. The report found that 26%, which equates to an estimated 71.9 million US adults, are currently spending nothing on European fashion, representing a potentially untapped market of $15.7Bn**.
Shipping costs, confusing sizing, returns, delivery times, and customs are among the obstacles that approximately 215 million shoppers face, while one in ten say they can’t buy from a European fashion brand because it doesn’t ship to the US.
In fact, the research shows that when Americans do discover and buy European fashion, online retailers (25%), department stores (21%) and US-based brand websites (21%) are the most common routes.
For European brands, the findings show a clear gap between demand and availability, says Dan Cate, CEO and Founder of SoldThrough.
He comments: “American consumers are telling us they value what European fashion brands bring to the market, and millions are already spending with them. But a consumer may know the brand, want the product, and believe it offers something different from what is available domestically, and still abandon the purchase if delivery is too expensive, sizing is unclear, or returning an item is difficult.
“The US is the world’s biggest apparel market, worth more than $373 billion, so the opportunity is clear, but too many European brands are making customers work too hard to buy from them.
“For UK and European brands looking to enter the US market, this is about understanding that the US customer expects to shop differently. Having the right retail channels, fulfilment and customer experience in place can make the difference between someone being interested in a brand and actually buying from it.”
The findings form part of SoldThrough’s ‘State of the US Fashion Market’ research study, which looks to identify how US consumers feel about UK and European Brands.

items.title: Supermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish within a decade
items.summary: Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons have set industry tongues wagging, with analysts saying the market is ripe for change Tesco lifts profit forecast and says shoppers are resilient They may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda or Morrisons – or both – could disappear within a decade. This week, it emerged that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons – the UK’s second- and sixth-largest supermarket chains – had held merger talks between last November and February, before the larger player decided to walk away. Continue reading...
items.body:
They may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda or Morrisons – or both – could disappear within a decade.
This week, it emerged that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons – the UK’s second- and sixth-largest supermarket chains – had held merger talks between last November and February, before the larger player decided to walk away.
News of the potential deal has relaunched speculation that the UK grocery market is now ripe for consolidation and revealed that the Sainsbury’s boss, Simon Roberts – who has been in post for six years – is at least willing to consider the possibility of buying one of his troubled rivals.
Sainsbury’s, which has 600 supermarkets and almost 900 convenience stores, has until recently been seen as wary of trying to revive merger talks with its rivals after its bid to buy Asda for £7bn in 2019 was blocked.
However, industry experts say Asda and Morrisons’ owners have held informal talks with each other – and both with Sainsbury’s team – and predict that talks could restart.
“The three of them, one way or another, are talking to each other,” one said. He suggested that a combination of Asda and Morrisons could happen but was likely to be a weaker deal than a Sainsbury’s takeover of either, as both businesses struggle with costs and interest on debt piles.
Competition fears ease
The industry has undergone significant change since the collapse of the Sainsbury’s-Asda deal. While riding the wider retail trends towards online shopping and convenience stores, the supermarket groups have been jockeying for market share.
Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket, with less than 1 percentage point separating them. Aldi is rapidly opening stores while Asda has struggled to find growth since a £6.8bn, debt-fuelled takeover in 2020 and heavy price competition from the discounters and from its bigger rivals Tesco and Sainsbury’s.
Another big change could emerge this month when the UK’s competition watchdog is due to publish its final ruling on whether Aldi and Lidl should now officially be classified as “large grocery retailers” like Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons.
In August, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it had found provisionally that Aldi and Lidl no longer qualified as “limited assortment discounters” as they now carry a “full range” of groceries and operate stores larger than 1,000 sq m (10,700 sq ft) across the UK.
The change means the German-owned discounters are now taken into account when assessing competition in different locations.
This is the strongest hint yet that the CMA has changed its stance blocking the Sainsbury’s buyout of Asda on the basis that shoppers would be worse off.
It also indicates that the CMA’s “balance of competition” – its estimation of the impact of a deal based on drive times for customers around stores – has shifted, meaning Sainsbury’s might have to dispose of dozens fewer stores to gain regulatory clearance for a merger. A figure of 150 was suggested when it tried to buy Asda.
Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital and Sainsbury’s broker, says the CMA preliminary ruling indicates “the shape of the pitch has adjusted a little” and “the change encourages another chapter of consolidation”.
It is a step-change from 2019 when analysts accused the singing former Sainsbury’s boss Mike Coupe and his board of directors of “arrogance” and “folly” for pursuing Asda. Now they say that consolidation is almost inevitable.
That comes amid what is seen as a more welcoming regulatory environment backed by the UK government’s growth agenda combined with the appointment of Doug Gurr, a grocery industry veteran who has spent time at Asda and Amazon, to lead the CMA.
Sainsbury’s holds the cards
One analyst described Sainsbury’s as the “kingmaker” in any industry consolidation as it uniquely has the resources to snap up a rival without the market dominance to immediately prevent any deal.
Analysts agree it is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy Morrisons or Asda – Tesco is too big to buy a rival, while Marks & Spencer and Waitrose appear unlikely to have the financial firepower or desire to pursue such a deal.
Amazon should not be ruled out as a player in consolidation, according to one analyst, who said the online specialist might be prompted into action by any of the supermarkets announcing plans to merge.
“The last cards are coming on to the table,” he said, suggesting that Amazon might consider buying Asda, Morrisons or even Sainsbury’s, now that it had effectively disposed of Argos which may have caused competition concerns for Amazon.
However, Amazon has not fared well with its dip into high street retail. Last year, it decided to close all 19 of its Fresh stores, with plans to convert five of them into shops under its Whole Foods Market brand.
As analysts at Bernstein put it: “We believe that scale is the most important source of advantage in grocery retail, and the combined market share of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would improve Sainsbury’s ability to take on Tesco.”
The logic of a deal for Morrisons’ American private equity owner is clear. Clayton, Dubilier & Rice has few options for an exit, four years on from its £7bn acquisition of the Bradford-based chain. Private equity bidders are not likely to be lining up, as there is little room for a another debt-fuelled buyout, while pursuing a stock market flotation would require a compelling growth story to lure investors but which is now absent.
The heavy debts taken on to fund CD&R’s acquisition in 2022 have left Morrisons struggling to compete as interest rates have risen, pushing up costs, while competition has toughened as pinched households look to save costs on their grocery bill.
Clearly, the CD&R adviser and former Tesco boss Terry Leahy is unlikely to let Morrisons go cheaply – with price demands ultimately understood to have led Sainsbury’s Roberts to walk away from any deal.
However, Morrisons has fallen back to be the UK’s sixth-largest supermarket with an 8.4% market share, just behind Lidl on 8.7%, according to the latest data from the industry analysts Worldpanel by Numerator.
A ‘sweetheart deal’
Asda’s owners, led by the British investment firm TDR Capital, may also welcome a tidy exit although they are likely to be happier to wait, having largely made their money selling off various parts of the grocer’s assets, industry insiders say. Under the returning boss, Allan Leighton, there are nascent signs of a turnaround if the owners are willing to sit tight and he does not appear keen on reviving talks with Sainsbury’s.
For Sainsbury’s, the appeal is cost-savings derived from larger scale. The combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would hold 23.6% of the UK market and add 500 supermarkets and 1,600 convenience stores to its portfolio – taking it closer to Tesco’s 27.8% market share. Buying Asda would take it to about 26.7%.
One industry expert said a combination with Asda was the “sweetheart deal” because it would not only bring larger scale but involve fewer stores serving the same customers in the south of the country.
The main benefit of any deal would come from cost-savings garnered from combining central operations, such as buying and property management, and aligning supplier terms.
Asda’s bigger supply chain brings greater potential savings and it is arguably a less complicated acquisition than Morrisons, which operates a large food processing business which Sainsbury’s would probably want to dispose of to a variety of specialist suppliers.
One issue is that businesses cannot seek pre-approval for a deal from the CMA, so launching a formal takeover offer for either Morrisons or Asda would involve an element of risk – consuming management time, and costly fees for bankers and lawyers.
As one industry expert says, “the critical argument is the role of the discounters” and the CMA’s rulings do not always follow the expected path. “It’s a lottery,” he said.
Analysts at Bernstein also say that “despite the benefits of a possible deal, the risk of distraction for Sainsbury’s would be high”.
The industry insider says: “Sainsbury’s is best served by being patient” as Asda and Morrisons are likely to continue to struggle. “There comes a point when the CMA has no choice but to let something happen as [Asda and Morrisons] can’t compete. You could argue that is already the case.”

items.body:
Peppa Pig gets Lionesses call-up as Football Association scores licensing deal with Hasbro
Peppa Pig maker Hasbro has struck a licensing deal with the Football Association that will see a new character, Libby Lioness, join the hit children’s animated TV show.
The agreement also covers the creation of co-branded merchandise and will launch next year, ahead of the European champions’ campaign at the 2027 Women’s World Cup in Brazil.
Former England international Jill Scott is to voice the character of Libby Lioness, who will make her debut in a two-part special next summer.
The move is a bid to convert young children into football fans “in a uniquely Peppa Pig way”, toys and games giant Hasbro said.
“England teams have inspired generations of young fans, and this initiative gives us an exciting new way to connect with children and families through one of the world’s most-loved preschool brands,” said FA head of licensing Marvin Farrell.
“We are delighted to be bringing the spirit of England and the world of Peppa Pig together through content and products in 2027 and beyond.”
Peppa Pig x Lionesses range of toys and clothing
As well as the TV show, Libby Lioness will appear in Peppa Pig Tales YouTube episodes and other branded digital content.
Products set to feature in the Peppa Pig x Lionesses range include toys, sporting accessories and clothing.
“Bringing Peppa Pig and England together is a truly exciting moment for the brand,” said Hasbro franchising chief Esra Cafer.
“Both celebrate confidence, resilience, friendship and the courage to try something new, making this a natural fit.
“With original content, consumer products, and retail all working together, we’re creating meaningful ways for young fans and families to connect with the game in a uniquely Peppa Pig way.”
It is not the first tie-up between England Women and a toy manufacturer, after Mattel created a Barbie doll in the image of Lioness Chloe Kelly earlier this year.

items.title: Superdrug teams up with Faye Winter for safer aesthetics campaign
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. The findings come as Superdrug prepares to launch Back Street To High Street in partnership with Save Face, a new campaign calling for greater safety and accountability […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
More than half of consumers believe proper qualifications, stronger regulation and rigorous clinical standards are critical to delivering safe and effective aesthetic treatments, new research from Superdrug reveals.
The findings come as Superdrug prepares to launch Back Street To High Street in partnership with Save Face, a new campaign calling for greater safety and accountability in the UK non-surgical aesthetics industry and positioning proper, face-to-face consultations as an essential first step before treatments such as dermal fillers and Botox.
New consumer research commissioned by Superdrug found:
- 54% say clear information about risks and expected results before treatment is critical to a safe and effective aesthetics service
- 53% want strong regulation and licensing of clinics and practitioners
- 52% say safe, approved products and equipment are critical
- 52% want strict hygiene and clinical safety standards in clinics
- 51% believe practitioners should have proper medical training and qualifications
The research also suggests consumers want responsibility for safety to sit with professionals and authorities rather than patients themselves. Almost two thirds (63%) believe government regulators or professional medical bodies should be responsible for ensuring the safety of aesthetic procedures in the UK, compared with just 9% who believe responsibility should fall to consumers themselves.
Superdrug’s Back Street To High Street campaign aims to help make aesthetics safer by championing the consultation and cooling off period as the crucial first steps in any treatment journey. The campaign is being launched alongside Superdrug’s charity partner Save Face, an organisation which supports people seeking non-surgical cosmetic treatments to find appropriately qualified and safe practitioners.
Save Face data shows the potential consequences when this crucial first step is missed, with 68% of complaints made to the organisation attributed to a lack of face-to-face consultation which led to negative outcomes.
Superdrug’s Aesthetics Clinic is designed to give customers greater confidence and reassurance when considering aesthetic treatments, with care delivered by qualified healthcare professionals within established clinical governance frameworks. Its clinicians are accredited by the Joint Council for Cosmetic Practitioners (JCCP), with both clinics and clinicians also accredited by Save Face. Superdrug Aesthetics Clinics hyperhidrosis service is regulated by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) in England and clinics in Scotland by Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS) helping to ensure consistent standards of quality, safety and patient care.
Chloe Saunders, head of healthcare services at Superdrug, said: “Aesthetic treatments have become increasingly mainstream, and so safety and clinical standards must keep pace. Our research shows that people want greater reassurance around who is treating them, the standards they can expect and the potential outcomes of treatment. A proper face-to-face consultation is fundamental to the entire journey. It gives people the opportunity to ask questions, understand the risks and expected results, and have an open conversation with a qualified healthcare professional about whether a treatment is actually right for them, and the appropriate route to take.”
“Through our Back Street To High Street campaign, we want to help raise expectations of what safe, responsible aesthetics should look like. By bringing professionally delivered aesthetic services into a trusted high street healthcare environment, we can help make high clinical standards more visible, accessible and expected across the industry to improve patient outcomes.”
Faye Winter, campaign ambassador and aesthetics safety advocate, added, ‘Having aesthetics treatments shouldn’t feel as simple as grabbing a coffee. These are medical procedures, and decisions that deserve the same care and attention as any other medical choice. I’ve seen first-hand how much confidence a safe procedure can give someone, but also experienced myself what can happen when people don’t understand the risks, or experience a negative outcome. That’s why I’m so thrilled to be part of Superdrug’s ‘Back Street To High Street’ campaign in partnership with Save Face. A proper consultation and cooling-off period are vital first steps that stand between someone making an informed decision and someone doing something they don’t fully understand. Everyone deserves that protection.’
Superdrug’s Back Street To High Street campaign reflects Superdrug’s wider commitment to championing safety, transparency and informed decision-making within the aesthetics industry. Customers visiting Superdrug’s Aesthetics Clinics receive an individual clinical consultation before treatment is considered, allowing them to discuss their needs, potential risks and expected outcomes with a qualified healthcare professional. items.body:
Dreams, the UK’s most loved bed retailer, is funding the first-ever extended opening hours of Mind’s Infoline, giving people access to mental health information and support 24 hours a day over World Mental Health Day weekend. The initiative forms part of Dreams’ three-year charity partnership with Mind and SAMH (Scottish Action for Mental Health).
Mental health problems don’t keep to a schedule, and for the first time, Mind’s Infoline will remain open continuously from 6pm on Friday 9 October until 9am on Monday 12 October, with the extended hours funded by Dreams.
The Infoline already supports around 100,000 people every year, providing vital information on mental health problems, where to get help, treatment options and people’s rights when accessing support. Over World Mental Health Day weekend, people will be able to speak to Mind’s trained advisors whether it is 2am or 2pm.
Alongside funding the extended Infoline hours, Dreams will donate £5 from every purchase made between 9 and 12 October to Mind and SAMH, across both its stores and online.
Dreams will also bring the conversation around sleep and mental health to The Cube at Battersea Power Station, with a public pop-up designed to explore some of the worries and pressures keeping people awake at night.
Live on Saturday 10th October (World Mental Health Day) from 10am-8pm, the activation will feature a bedroom installation bringing to life key messages from Dreams and Mind, alongside a digital projection exploring what keeps people up at night, based on new research commissioned by Dreams. Wellness expert Emma Mills will be available throughout the activation, offering mini drop-in sessions where visitors can explore mindfulness, journaling and meditation techniques, while Dreams’ trained Mental Health First Aiders will be on hand for anyone who would like to talk, offering support and signposting visitors to relevant resources and services.
Siobhan King, chief marketing officer at Dreams, said: “Helping people sleep better is what we’re all about at Dreams, and we know how closely connected sleep and mental health are. For a lot of people, it’s at nighttime when worries feel their loudest and it can be hardest to switch off.
That’s why I’m really proud that Dreams is funding extended opening hours for Mind’s Infoline over the World Mental Health Day weekend.
Together with our £5 donation from every purchase and our Battersea Power Station installation, we want to use World Mental Health Day to encourage people to open up and have more open conversations about mental health, all while raising funds for Mind and SAMH.”
Neeleema Boodhram, helplines manager at Mind, said: “Through our services we know that mental health problems don’t keep to a schedule, and neither do the worries, questions and challenges that can come with them. Dream’s funding to keep Mind’s Infoline open throughout the World Mental Health Day weekend will make a real difference to those that reach out to us for support. This weekend, our trusted information and support will be available whenever they need it, day or night.”.”

As the first dedicated supermarket aisle of its kind in the UK, Simple Ingredients features over 350 branded products made with recognisable ingredients and no […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
In response to customer demand, Ocado Retail has launched Simple Ingredients, a dedicated online aisle featuring a curated selection of products made only with ingredients customers are likely to recognise.
As the first dedicated supermarket aisle of its kind in the UK, Simple Ingredients features over 350 branded products made with recognisable ingredients and no artificial additives such as colours, emulsifiers, stabilisers or flavours.
The launch comes as new research reveals strong demand for simpler, more transparent food choices, with nearly three quarters (74%) of UK consumers preferring products containing ingredients they recognise.
The new aisle simplifies shopping by making it easier for customers to identify products they might use in their own kitchen. Almost two thirds (65%) say shopping would be easier if they could quickly identify foods with fewer added ingredients, while over half (51%) find it difficult to know what ingredients have been added to the foods they buy.
This uncertainty is changing grocery shopping habits. Nearly three in five consumers (57%) are looking at ingredient labels more closely than they were a year ago, while almost half (48%) have changed what they buy based on information about ingredients.
The findings also reveal the confusion and time pressures shoppers face. More than half (54%) struggle to keep up with changing advice about food and ingredients, while half (50%) say they do not have time to check the label or ingredients of every product they buy.
Social media plays a particularly prominent role among younger shoppers, with almost two in five Gen Z consumers (39%) using it for information about food ingredients – more than double the national average of 19% – yet 60% find it difficult to tell which food information online they can trust.
Ocado’s own search data reflects this growing interest, with searches for ‘unprocessed’ up 178% year on year, ‘wholefood’ up 133% and ‘natural’ up 59%.
To make these products easier to find, the Simple Ingredients aisle brings them together in one dedicated destination on Ocado.com. Available all year round and updated seasonally, the aisle spans everyday favourites including frozen pizzas, burgers and ready meals; ketchup, salad dressings and sauces; breads, cereals and baked goods; and ice cream, snacks and treats.
The aisle will also feature products from the M&S Only range, which are made with eight or fewer ingredients and free from artificial colours or preservatives. Searches have risen 1,533% year on year since the range launched in March 2025, underlining strong demand for products with simpler ingredient lists.
Charlie Parker, senior nutritionist at Ocado Retail, said: “Customers increasingly want to know what is in the food they buy, but navigating ingredient lists can be difficult and time-consuming. We have checked the back of every pack so customers do not have to, bringing together products made with recognisable ingredients in one dedicated aisle, while leaving them to make an informed choice about what works for them as part of their overall diet.”
The Simple Ingredients criteria is based on recognisable ingredients only and does not guarantee a healthier diet. Ocado recommends following the Eatwell Guide and checking product nutrition labels to help make informed dietary choices as part of a varied and balanced diet.
Customers can browse the aisle on Ocado.com here.

items.title: Asos hackers duped employee in data breach
items.summary: The hackers behind a threat to leak Asos customer data duped an employee by posing as a “trusted contact,” the fast-fashion group has said. An unknown group shocked Asos’ millions of customers on Tuesday when they published a push notification on the online retailer’s app, claiming to have hacked into the company and threatening a [...]
items.body:
Asos hackers duped employee in data breach
The hackers behind a threat to leak Asos customer data duped an employee by posing as a “trusted contact,” the fast-fashion group has said.
An unknown group shocked Asos’ millions of customers on Tuesday when they published a push notification on the online retailer’s app, claiming to have hacked into the company and threatening a data leak.
The incident triggered an immediate sell-off of the London-listed group, as its shares fell more than 13 per cent, casting doubt on the company’s ability to continue its turnaround plan.
Asos told customers on Thursday morning that it has launched a “detailed investigation” into the incident, apologising for the “uncertainty” caused by the notification. The update was the group’s first message directly to shoppers since the hack.
The fashion group said: “We discovered that an unauthorised party gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain login credentials.
“Those credentials were then used to access information on certain third-party platforms used by Asos.”
The company said it immediately locked down its platforms to prevent further activity and has referred the incident to “the relevant law enforcement and regulatory authorities”.
The e-commerce firm reassured its customers that the hackers did not access any payment information or passwords, though they did obtain “some personal information, including names and contact details”.
Asos said: “Once our investigation is complete, we will contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required.
“We know our customers trust us with their information. We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls. Thank you for your patience and for continuing to put your trust in us.”
Asos says app safe to use
Shares in FTSE-250-listed Asos ticked up following the group’s statement, gaining four per cent to 469p.
Asos users were alerted to the hack on Tuesday when a notification appeared on customers’ phones, saying: “Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it.”
Snowflake is a cloud platform used to process data like clothing sizes and body measurements. It also lets users send notifications to clients’ phones.
Snowflake denied that hackers gained access to its systems. A company spokesperson said on Tuesday that it found “no compromise” of its platform.
The notification included a link to a Telegram channel, where a user named ‘Xuanye Group’ said it had obtained customer information which is “safe” on their server and “will not be touched for a designated period”.
“Considering the current situation regarding incident disclosure in the cyber security landscape, you can thank us for our generous clarity regarding this incident,” they added.
British retailers have faced several cyberattacks in recent years. Last year, IT workers at Marks and Spencer were tricked by hackers who gained access to the retailer’s systems.
Asos is in the midst of a turnaround under chief executive José Antonio Ramos Calamonte. Last month, the fast fashion firm said it is on track to beat its 48-50 per cent gross margin target and its forecast of between £150m and £180m adjusted earnings.
Charles Allen, an analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said the hack “may temporarily cap the pace” of the company’s turnaround. “The loss of customer trust could weigh on efforts to rebuild its client base,” he said.

items.title: Freemans unveils major rebrand with renewed focus on UK’s £92bn 40+ female market

Digital department store Freemans today (8th October 2026) revealed a new brand platform that leans into its 121-year heritage and is designed specifically to appeal to the over-40 female shopper and her spending power. This evolution is designed to ensure both growth and relevance, helping this customer with her shopping needs across fashion, home and […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Digital department store Freemans today (8th October 2026) revealed a new brand platform that leans into its 121-year heritage and is designed specifically to appeal to the over-40 female shopper and her spending power.
This evolution is designed to ensure both growth and relevance, helping this customer with her shopping needs across fashion, home and beauty.
This single-minded approach has paid dividends, with the heritage brand undergoing a breakneck transformation from a catalogue stalwart to a digital pure-play retailer over the last few years, famously seeing it retire its ‘weighty’ then 118-year-old catalogue.
Even more impressively, while all this change was happening, the Bradford-based, company, Freemans delivered six years of consecutive growth, beating the performance of the wider market sector.
The new brand platform leans into both the outlook and nouse of these confident women, who spend a staggering £92 billion annually in the UK and directly steer 93% of all household purchasing decisions.
So confident is the retailer in its approach that it was also keen to align its internal teams to reflect this customer.
This started with the appointment of Ann Steer as CEO more than six years ago, who proudly sits within this age group. Its buying functions, led by Susie Calvert, also mirror the customer’s age profile, with womenswear, home and beauty departments reflecting the same. Even its marketing and creative teams are led by women in this age group. The approach, at such breadth, is unique and essential, claims Freemans.
A cleaner approach to look and feel saw Freemans delve back into its past for inspiration while examining today’s behavioural patterns of these confident consumers: money-smart women who skilfully juggle life’s to-do list while scouting, chatting to one another and curating their wardrobes and homes on a budget.
These women were historically at the heart of both Freemans’ success and affection, as far back as the 1960s, when tens of thousands were the face of the forward-thinking brand.
Affectionately called “Catalogue Ladies”, they took orders and payments from friends, families and neighbours while earning commission, all at a time when women could not get credit, loans or even mortgages in their own names without a male guarantor.
Customers will see a revitalised look and feel when visiting Freemans.com: easier to navigate, easier to shop and more inspirational, with the retailer’s famed handwritten “F” signature being brought back for the first time since the 1950s.
It has retired its bold Freemans mango-coloured logo in favour of a more subtle palette of greens, plums and the occasional fluorescent highlight to celebrate special deals and sales.
The shift also allows a more elevated editorial style of photography, with age-appropriate models showcasing both own-brand and third-party ranges.
Anchoring all of this is a new line: “Shopping is your department. And Freemans is your department store.”
The launch marks a major business milestone following a successful six-year structural migration, moving Freemans away from its old mail-order paper catalogues to become a thriving digital pure-play powerhouse serving an active base of more than one million customers across the UK, all while growing ahead of the wider market.
Ann Steer, Chief Executive at Freemans, said: “While much of the retail sector is focused on attracting the next generation of shoppers, we’ve remained steadfast in our commitment to a customer we know exceptionally well: women over 40, one of the most influential consumer groups in the UK.
“The modern 40+ female shopper has significant purchasing power, yet she is often underserved or portrayed through outdated stereotypes. Too often she’s labelled with terms like ‘Queenager’ or ‘Midster’, when the reality is that she’s confident, discerning and highly informed.
“I am one of these women, and I know she doesn’t need to be told who she is or how to shop. We’ve built relationships with this customer for more than 60 years and continue to learn from her every day. Today’s shopper researches carefully, compares options and understands value. She makes considered decisions and expects brands to respect her knowledge and experience.
“Our business strategy is anchored in a simple truth: ‘Shopping is your department. And Freemans is your department store’, with a single-minded focus on this woman. So serious is this commitment that all key business functions across buying, merchandising, beauty, home, creative and marketing are headed up by women of exactly the same age as the customer we serve.”
Six years of consecutive market-beating growth and crossing the million-customer mark proves all this is working. This new brand platform, which is not only customer-facing but attitudinal, percolates through our whole business and will be what sets us apart and will be the foundation of continued growth.”
Freemans is backing the launch with a multi-million-pound Q4 marketing campaign across connected TV, digital video, print and nationwide radio.
Freemans has partnered with an exclusive stable of Britain’s most trusted broadcasting icons who are a true testament to the modern woman over 40, including Zoe Ball, Gaby Roslin, Kate Thornton and Nicki Chapman.
Shunning the traditional approach of reading standard advertising scripts, these presenters will deliver pre-recorded host endorsements across major national radio networks including Greatest Hits Radio and Magic Radio. This activity is heavily weighted towards evening and weekend “second-screening” hours, reaching the audience precisely when they are browsing on secondary devices.
The campaign also includes: targeted advertorials in high-circulation women’s titles. Alongside a premium connected video rollout across YouTube, Discovery, Channel 5, Pluto TV and Samsung Ads, will complement the campaign, in addition to amplification across all Freemans owned channels.
The website overhaul: the cognitive science of colour
From paper to pixels, Freemans is using applied colour psychology to ease screen fatigue and make its new digital department store work for the way modern women actually browse.
Moving away from the cold, white, clinical grids used by most online retailers, the company has built its entire user interface around a calculated three-part colour system:
Signature Green: Used as the primary background colour. Grounded in cognitive science, this soft, organic green naturally lowers visual processing strain. On a smartphone screen, it eliminates the blinding glare of traditional white sites, turning a long evening browse into a comfortable wind-down.
Chocolate Plum: Replacing harsh black text, this rich and comforting plum shade ensures high typographic clarity while giving an upscale, premium look that is significantly softer on the eyes.
Fluorescent Highlights: A bright pop of energy used with absolute precision. Instead of overwhelming the customer with flashing sales banners, it acts as a quiet guide, steering her eye naturally towards key updates, special deals and checkout areas exactly when she needs them.

items.body:
Alibaba.com today announced the return of CoCreate Pitch Europe, its product-based start-up competition spotlighting the next generation of entrepreneurs.
Following the success of last year’s inaugural competition, CoCreate Pitch 2026 will take place in London from 19th-20th November with a star-studded panel of expert judges. Having been a judge in 2025, Rio Ferdinand OBE1 returns to lead the 2026 panel, which also features business guru Deborah Meaden2 and social media sensation Simon Squibb.
CoCreate Pitch 2026 is an AI-driven product innovation competition giving start-ups from across the globe the chance to be named Alibaba.com’s Grand Winner. Prizes come from a $1 million global prize pool shared across the competition’s US and European editions, each with its own Grand Winner.
Last year, 16-year-old Harrison Nott, founder of CoolTowel™, was crowned CoCreate Pitch 2025’s Europe Grand Winner. After meeting Harrison, Rio chose to stay involved, providing hands-on mentorship and business advice throughout the year. His continued involvement speaks to the connections CoCreate can spark.
Since winning the competition last year, Harrison has used his $200,000 prize money as fuel for expansion, scaling up operations and building out his support team, including logistics and customer service. Rio also opened doors that would otherwise have been out of reach, connecting Harrison with high-profile international networks and audiences and helping build the brand’s international profile. This combination of funding and mentorship has helped Harrison’s business grow tenfold, and earlier this year, he generated the equivalent of almost two-thirds of his entire annual revenue from the year before in a single day.
As well as Rio, this year’s competition finalists will get to meet Deborah Meaden, one of the UK’s most recognisable business voices, TV personality and serial investor. After a long career in the Leisure Industry, she finally exited her holiday business and became a full-time investor, backing over 50 fast growing and scaling businesses and giving her a breadth of experience and unrivalled understanding of the challenges facing today’s small business owners.
Rio and Deborah will sit alongside entrepreneur, author and social media sensation, Simon Squibb. Simon is a serial entrepreneur, angel investor, and author of the #1 Sunday Times bestselling book “What’s Your Dream?”. With over 22 million social media followers and 2 billion views each year across all his content, Simon has become a leading voice in entrepreneurship. Simon has invested in over 81 companies, including Lovable, Skillstore, and Stan, and has given away over £425,000 to support people chasing their dreams.
The trio will be joined by Jonathan Anguelov, co-founder of French unicorn Aircall and recognized among the top economic changemakers in France under 40.
Harrison Nott, CEO & founder, CoolTowel™, said: “Winning CoCreate Pitch last year has changed the trajectory of my business. It’s not just about the prize money, it’s about the connections and the platform it gives you to take your business to the next level.
“The network I built through CoCreate Pitch opened doors I could only have dreamed of, like getting CoolTowel™ in the hands of professional athletes and celebrities. The mentorship and practical business advice from Rio over the past nine months have been a gamechanger, and I would encourage anyone with a brilliant product idea to take the leap and enter CoCreate Pitch 2026. There’s nothing like it to scale your business.”
Kuo Zhang, president of Alibaba.com, said: “We are delighted to return to London and hear from some of Europe’s most exciting scale-ups as they pitch to win our significant prize package. Over the last year, the growth of Harrison’s business has exemplified the added value that CoCreate Pitch can provide entrepreneurs with, particularly when combined with advice and insight from our industry-leading judges, as well as our Alibaba.com and Accio teams.”
This year’s CoCreate Pitch is powered by Accio, which provides entrepreneurs with a pre-configured agentic AI business team that manages the entire SME lifecycle end to end, from market analysis, design and sourcing to store optimisation and inventory monitoring. And for this year’s competition, a dedicated ‘CoCreate Pitch Agent’ helps applicants transform early product ideas into structured pitch concepts and actionable business plans. Applications for the London event close on October 16, 2026. For more information, please visit the CoCreate Pitch event page.
The announcement comes as new data from Alibaba.com and Small Business Institute Research6 shows that only 5% of small business owners are using agentic AI for supply chain management. It also shows that while only 5% are using agentic AI regularly, 68% of UK entrepreneurs want to find out more about what it can do for their business.

- Exmouth, Devon
- Halifax, West Yorkshire

items.body:
Napolina, the UK’s largest selling ambient Italian food brand, has announced a major six-figure ATL investment to further bolster its strong market growth.
The much-loved brand is seeking to capitalise on recent successes with a high-impact national OOH and YouTube advertising campaign, running throughout October and November, as it aims to bring a taste of Italy to more British tables.
The launch is set to support Napolina’s upward trajectory in recent years, with growth of 13.7% over the last two years in value. As shoppers increasingly seek authentic ingredients with trusted provenance, Napolina continues to earn consumer confidence through its commitment to quality. Rooted in Italy’s rich culinary heritage, the brand’s focus on premium ingredients and meaningful innovation has helped drive growth ahead of the wider market.
Napolina is shifting its investment towards high-impact advertising. With YouTube now the second most-watched service in the UK, behind the BBC and ahead of ITV, this will enable the brand to connect with modern, at-home cooks at crucial moments throughout their shopping journey.
Napolina’s award-winning ‘Your Bolognaise will Thank You’ creative will take centre stage across OOH, putting the chopped tomato can firmly – and rightly so – in the spotlight. The creative highlights the importance of the humble, tinned tomato, emphasising that quality is the secret to elevating everyday dinners. The campaign champions the idea that all great Italian meals start with great tomatoes.
YouTube will premiere a brand-new concept that heroes at-home cooks with ‘Now you’re cooking’. The humorous, light-hearted creative aims to celebrate the enthusiasm and ambition of Britain’s home cooks. Napolina’s new advert follows a confident, at-home chef as he passionately demonstrates how to make the perfect spag bol and why choosing the right tomato is so crucial. The story takes an unexpected twist as his car is towed away and we see that his culinary expertise does not extend to parking restrictions, proving that the best cooks can’t be experts at everything.
The OOH investment will target high-footfall locations including UK train stations Liverpool Central, Liverpool Lime Street, Manchester Piccadilly, Kings Cross and Birmingham New Street as well as roadside large formats at Fulham Broadway, Hammersmith Broadway, Gypsy Corner, Trinity Way and Grand Central Birmingham.
Additionally, D48 billboards will be in proximity to local stockists such as Liverpool’s Stanley Road, near the Sainsbury’s on Great Homer Street, and Prescot Road near the Tesco.
Running throughout October and November 2026, the adverts reinforce Napolina as the go-to choice for shoppers seeking quality Italian ingredients they know and trust, as consumers continue to prioritise authenticity and provenance.
Jeremy Gibson, marketing director at Princes Group PLC, commented: “Napolina’s continued growth reflects the increasing demand for trusted, authentic Italian brands in the UK, which is testament to our not so humble confidence and the momentum we’ve built. This six-figure investment into the brand, across a two-year period, represents a significant milestone for us. After three years without significant ATL support, we’re demonstrating our commitment to Napolina, our retail partners, and crucially, to our consumers by making a bold statement about our ambitions.
“Our target audience of passionate at-home chefs are increasingly turning to platforms like YouTube for food inspiration, recipe ideas and cooking tips. By focusing purely on high-impact OOH and YouTube, instead of traditional TV, we’re reaching home cooks exactly where they are, with a campaign that celebrates the joy and creativity of cooking with Napolina.”
Napolina is continuing to invest and innovate across the range, reflected in its newly launched Pasta Stir-Ins, which offers an alternative to traditional pasta sauce. Available in four flavours, they can be effortlessly stirred through cooked, hot pasta including plain and filled varieties.

items.title: Some ‘less-healthy’ products not captured by promotion rules, according to report
items.summary: Foods that the public overwhelmingly regards as unhealthy, including burgers and crisps, are not being captured by the advertising and supermarket promotion restrictions because the UK is still relying on nutrition rules developed more than 20 years ago, according to new analysis from the Obesity… This story continues at Some ‘less-healthy’ products not captured by promotion rules, according to report Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
In its latest snapshot, OHA compared how products are classified as ‘healthy‘ or ‘less healthy’ under the government’s current 2004/05 Nutrient Profiling Model (current NPM) and the 2018 NPM (updated model).
The analysis found that six of the seven food and drink products currently allowed to be advertised during the Britain’s Got Talent Final, a popular family viewing programme, could be reclassified as ‘less healthy’ under the updated NPM.
A similar gap emerged on supermarket shelves. 45 out of the 68 in-scope products featured in promotions at the end-of-aisle, such as cakes and biscuits, sugary drinks and desserts and puddings, that currently pass the current NPM could be classed as ‘less healthy’ under the updated NPM.
That disconnect is also reflected in what the public thinks. In polling conducted by Savanta among a nationally representative sample of 2,211 UK adults, 77% described a KFC Zinger Burger as unhealthy, 71% said the same of a McDonald’s Spicy McCrispy and 62% of Walkers Prawn Cocktail crisps.
Yet, these products can still fall outside the advertising and promotion restrictions under the current NPM. This, says OHA, highlights a gap between the rules, latest evidence, and public understanding.
More than two-thirds of adults (69%) believe children regularly see advertising for unhealthy food and drink, while 57% say the government should do more to restrict it.
This is despite the government introducing long-awaited laws to stop less healthy food being advertised before 9 pm on TV and through paid-for online media at any time.
The OHA is now urging ministers to move quickly to implement both the updated Nutrient Profiling Model and the Healthy Food Standard. It is calling on the government to:
- Publish its response to the consultation on applying the updated NPM, which is already past the 12 weeks recommended by government guidance.
- Publish the consultation on the Healthy Food Standard immediately, enabling businesses to prepare for and implement mandatory healthy sales reporting and improvement targets.
- Implement the updated NPM and the Healthy Food Standard as soon as possible, within this Parliament, in line with the Health and Social Care Select Committee’s recommendations
Katharine Jenner, executive director of the Obesity Health Alliance, said: “Families expect the rules on food advertising and promotions to reflect modern nutrition science. Instead, we’re still relying on a model designed more than 20 years ago.
“Both the updated model and the Healthy Food Standard were promised in the NHS 10‑Year Plan, and countries around the world are already modernising how they identify unhealthy products based on the latest evidence – so multinational companies have long known which way the wind is blowing.
“Now they need to be implemented quickly, so the rules make sense to businesses, parents and consumers, and help ensure the food we buy is affordable, available and advertised responsibly.”

Stick a puffin in your pocket: Bank of England reveals animals to replace Churchill and other historical figures on banknotes... but why has the kingfisher missed out?
Puffins, owls, bumblebees and hedgehogs will replace historical figures such as Winston Churchill on the Bank of England's next series of banknotes.
It comes after nearly half a million people took part in a controversial consultation to choose which animals should appear on Britain's paper money.
The move raises the questions of whether cash-strapped friends will perhaps be asking each other to 'lend us a puffin' or if they can 'spare a hedgehog' as the new notes are introduced over the next few years.
It ends a tradition going back to 1970 of featuring historical figures – starting with William Shakespeare – on UK banknotes.
And the decision to switch to animals has prompted major backlash, being described as a 'total bonkers' while Tory leader Kemi Badenoch complained the move was 'erasing our history'.
The four animals have been chosen after being whittled down from a shortlist of 18 announced earlier this year.
The Atlantic puffin will be included on bank notes 'to celebrate the British coastline'
They will feature on the £5, £10, £20 and £50 but it has not yet been decided which. Other animals could also appear on the eventual designs. The banknote series will continue to feature a portrait of the monarch.
The month-long public consultation received 478,531 responses – the most ever for a banknote. Respondents placed 2,549,003 selections across the shortlist.
The humble buff-tailed bumblebee topped the list with 360,399 votes, more than 100,000 ahead of the European hedgehog on 256,665.
In third was the barn owl with 270,596. The Atlantic puffin came in sixth place with 183,137 but was selected above more popular animals because Bank officials decided that 'the inclusion of a marine animal will add variety to the series' and 'provide an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline'.
That meant the red fox with 244,651 votes and the common kingfisher with 211,277 missed out.
The animals will replace the current designs featuring Winston Churchill on the £5 note, Jane Austen on the £10, JMW Turner on £20 and Alan Turing on the £50 note.
The Bank said it would take a number of years to design, test and print the banknotes 'to make sure they are high-quality, resilient and accessible'.
Chief cashier Victoria Cleland said: 'I am delighted that nearly half a million people responded to our wildlife imagery consultation, showing that cash still matters.
'We have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes.'
The Bank has said that while the use of cash for transactions has declined over the past decade, it remains the preferred payment method for about one in seven people and is used by many more.
Cash in circulation has continued to increase, reaching £91.5billion at the end of February 2026.
The Bank has previously run into controversy over banknote designs after campaigners complained that too few women had featured in recent years, prior to Jane Austen being added to the £10 note in 2017.
Its history has also proved uncomfortable due to links with slavery. In 2021, the Bank removed a series of paintings and busts of governors and directors from display as they had connections to the slave trade in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

items.title: Tesco predicts a low-alcohol ‘healthier’ Christmas
items.summary: First-half sales rise 2% to £33.8bn, helped by strong trade online, as retailer says it is making more delivery slots available Supermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish Tesco has raised its profit outlook as it expects households to splash out this Christmas – despite buying less alcohol – as they shrug off “uncertainty” over the Iran war. The UK’s biggest grocer said sales rose just 2% to £33.8bn in the 26 weeks to 29 August, but underlying profit was up 6.5% to £1.8bn. Continue reading...
items.body:
Tesco has raised its profit outlook as it expects households to splash out this Christmas – despite buying less alcohol – as they shrug off “uncertainty” over the Iran war.
The UK’s biggest grocer said sales rose just 2% to £33.8bn in the 26 weeks to 29 August, but underlying profit was up 6.5% to £1.8bn.
Ken Murphy, the chief executive of Tesco, said growth had been helped by strong online sales, which were up 8%, and a 9% jump in revenue from its premium own-label Finest range.
He said: “Consumers in the UK have been pretty resilient in an uncertain environment and there is a sense that customers want to enjoy Christmas, given everything that is going on in the world.”
The retailer had bought more stock of “key Christmas lines”, understood to be foods such as turkey and mince pies, and added 10% more delivery slots for its online grocery business. It is also ramping up its in-house rapid delivery service, Whoosh, and has signed new partnerships, including with Deliveroo.
Murphy said he expected Britons to seek out a “marginally healthier Christmas” with higher sales of low-alcohol and no-alcohol drinks, including ready-mixed mocktails, but that families would still treat themselves as “customers do love to indulge”.
He said he was not expecting food supplies to be hit by this summer’s drought. Tesco had also hedged its energy costs into next year and was making savings across the business to help keep prices down for shoppers.
He said the business still had room for growth despite being almost twice the size of its nearest rival, Sainsbury’s, with a 28% market share, and that he did not “dwell too much” on the possibility of its closest rival acquiring another leading supermarket.
Sainsbury’s is understood to have walked away from merger talks in January with the UK’s sixth-biggest supermarket, Morrisons, prompting consolidation chatter across the industry.
“Whatever happens in the market we will respond to it,” Murphy said. While Tesco is expanding its reach with financial services and more fashion, he said its strategy “begins and ends in winning in food”.
The company added: “While consumer confidence has remained relatively resilient in the first half of the year, ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to create uncertainty and we remain focused on helping customers get the best possible value.”
Earlier this year, Tesco warned that profits could fall in the year ahead, citing increased uncertainty caused by the conflict in Iran, which began in late February. However, some economic indicators have suggested that the war has not yet had a significant impact. Last week, official estimates for UK growth in the second quarter were upgraded.
The company said it now expected to make underlying annual profits of between £3.15bn and £3.3bn. That represents an upgrade from its previous expectation of at least £3bn in profits but the bottom end of the range would still mark a fall from a year earlier.
Sales at established UK Tesco stores were up 1.5% as food sales motored, but the group’s Booker wholesale arm continued to struggle, with sales falling 2.6%.
The supermarket said it was increasingly using artificial intelligence across the business, including in a meal-planning assistant that was tested from April with 280,000 staff before being launched for customers in September.
It said AI was also helping to cut costs by making in-store stock replenishment more efficient and improving energy efficiency in its supermarkets.
Tesco shares rose 4% on Thursday morning.
