Including Dunelm, Toolstation, Bodycare: 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards physical retail finalists announced
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Bricks and Mortar Retail category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
Our 2026 Bricks and Mortar Retail finalists as follows:
Shortlist:
Bodycare and PMC
Bought out of administration in 2025, Bodycare has worked with PMC on an innovation driven store opening programme to bring its affordable health and beauty offering back to the high street, aiming to open 25 UK stores in 2026 and 200 by 2031.
Dunelm and Enactor
Dunelm has turned self-checkout from a small idea in 2023 into a core part of its stores, with assisted self-service now 85% rolled out across the estate. Instead of an off the shelf SCO, Dunelm built its own on the Enactor platform, running the same software as its tills.
Dunelm's own teams use the Enactor Toolkit to design and change the journey, adding real-time colleague headset alerts, a pin audio prompt and layouts that flex by store size.
Paul Smith and Sitoo
Paul Smith has transformed the role of technology in its physical stores with Sitoo’s Unified Commerce Platform, anchored by PoS. Rolled out across 30+ stores in eight countries in three months, the platform gives associates greater freedom to serve customers anywhere in the store using mPoS.
Pharma&Go and Sensei
Pharma&GO turns a 70 m² store in Lisbon into a health shop that never closes. Opposite Hospital CUF Descobertas, it is 100% autonomous and open 24/7: customers check in with a bank card, pick up what they need and walk out, with payment charged automatically. There are no checkouts, no queues and no staff on site.
Toolstation and eLocker
Toolstation has reimagined Click and Collect at its Toolstation GO Battersea store through a new 24/7 smart locker service developed with eLocker.
Waitrose and SOLUM
Waitrose and SOLUM are delivering a UK wide digital shelf transformation using Newton Pro electronic shelf labels. Following pilots, the programme has expanded to more than 200 stores and over three million labels.

items.body:
Grocery firm Asda and Rokt partner to bring AI tech powered relevant offers to customers at checkout
Asda has partnered with Rokt to deliver relevant offers to the UK grocery retailer’s customers at checkout across its online grocery business and George, its clothing and home brand. Using Rokt Pay+ on the payment page and Rokt Thanks on the order confirmation page, Asda says it has created a new retail media revenue stream at the point of purchase, while customer conversion remains unchanged.
Rokt uses AI to determine the most relevant next action for each customer in real-time on both the payments and confirmation pages.
“Checkout is a critical part of the customer journey, so we were deliberate about how we approached it,” says Chris Chalmers, Vice President Customer Data and Loyalty at Asda “The results show we can make that experience more relevant for customers while creating meaningful new value for the business.”
Asda first launched Rokt Thanks on George’s order confirmation page in January 2025. It added Rokt Pay+ to the payment page and then expanded both products across its online grocery business. The results include: Rokt revenue on George more than doubled after Rokt Pay+ was added. Pay+ now makes up 51% of Rokt revenue on George, and 36% across groceries and George. Rokt revenue on Asda's grocery business grew 54% year on year, based on a 30-day comparison. Customer conversion was unaffected across both businesses.
“The payment page is one of the highest intent moments in e-commerce, but historically it’s been largely untapped,” says Courtney Hopkins, SVP of Strategic Partnerships at Rokt
“Asda is showing that retailers can improve the experience for customers, thereby creating meaningful incremental value in that moment. We look forward to continuing to innovate and grow the partnership to unlock even greater relevance throughout the e-commerce journey and potentially even customer acquisition.”

items.body:
FT Live Future of Retail Summit review: how can retailers compete in the TikTok and Instagram economy?
Social media and commerce is a “ferocious and hungry beast” that constantly needs feeding with up to 700 pieces of content per month, reflected Taymoor Atighetchi, CEO and Founder at digital stationers’ Papier, which is opening its first physical store next year, at the FT Live 2026 Future of Retail event in the City of London this week.
It’s a sentiment fellow panellist, David Abrahamovitch, CEO at Grind, a UK coffee and accessories seller, which has undergone the opposite journey from shops to online in the omnichannel space that Papier is now targeting, agreed with during a conference session entitled: How Retailers Can Compete in the TikTok & Instagram Economy?
“We actually do most of our social commerce on Meta’s Facebook or the Google platform,” said Abrahamovitch at FT Live Future of Retail. “Partly because we know we’ll get return on investment on that.”
“We do use Tik Tok itself, but not so much TikTok Shop. That is a very different animal,” continued Abrahamovitch, as he reflected on how Grind has been burned in the past and learnt how it can be somewhat of a price centric clearing house, which might be OK for a fashion retailer trying to offload unseasonal clothes but isn’t suitable for a premium coffee brand selling evergreen products.
“I’d also advise against getting too excited chasing customer acquisitions with fantastic new joiner offerings as we’ve learnt they don’t stay and become long-term valuable customers.”
“Pick your viral moments too and control your narrative,” he added, while admitting it’s no good producing expensive polished content anymore that isn’t recognised when it’s chucked into a modern algorithms, such as Meta’s Andromeda.
Andromeda stain
This algo adversely impacted ranking prerequisites when it was introduced by Meta on Instagram and elsewhere with little warning recently. It helped to fuel the digital retail sector’s move towards having to produce ever more content than was previously necessary to get rankings and sales, negating the quality for the quantity to feed the beast as it were.
The ferocious nature of the social commerce beast was perhaps best recognised by the absence of Vanessa Spence, EVP of Brand & Creative at Asos, who was due to be part of the panel at FT Live Retail 2026, but withdrew as the fast fashion giant suffered a high profile cyber attack on 6th October.
“Lower product quality and ‘unboxing type videos’ that can be made on your phone seemed to be prioritised by Meta’s new Andromeda algo, which isn’t what a premium retailer like us wants,” said Atighetchi, while admitting that his company still had to play the game to remain relevant. “TikTok Shop is a QVC style deal shop channel as well,” he said, agreeing with his fellow panellist that “the D2C gold rush era is over” and socials have become harder more recently. Andromeda seems to favour lower product and content quality in terms of pricing and ‘unboxing type videos’ that can be made on your phone.
“It’s a volume game now. We also seed - i.e. give away free product - to people who we know will make new content for us and reach their followers. It’s cost effective.”
Risk factors
The risk of being unprepared when a social platform changes its algo are evident, but the panellists at FT Live Retail 2026 also discussed insisting on ROI and being aware of returns cost and fraud as issues.
“We saw hundreds of deliveries to one address in a high rise block of flats in London,” said Abrahamovitch, when sharing too generous customer acquisition first time customer learnings. However, Grind still plays the game and creates “viral moments” via aligning with Coffee Week and so on and collaborating with artists, Pokémon and so on to get social traction and customers.
It seems that feeding the beast and the cost benefit analysis of social commerce is still worth it. But Abrahamovitch did advise diversifying “so you’re not overly reliant on one platform or channel”. His store led initial opening phase also helps to build trust and loyalty with customers which is paradoxically more important than ever in a digital era - if you don’t want to compete on just price alone.
“Trust does still matter,” concurred Atighetchi, while concluding: “Social media has its place, but we are all using it too much.” Amen to that! But equally it isn’t going away, especially in an era of agentic AI led commerce where a firm’s control over its data quality and product listings will be more important than ever when aiming to get to the top of an agent’s ranking, rather than just an SEO engine or a social platform’s algo.

Grocery retailer Panda teams with Spike and GoWit to power e-commerce media push in Saudi Arabia
Panda Retail, a grocery retailer in Saudi Arabia, has partnered with Spike Media Saudi, GoWit’s partner in the region, operating locally as GoSpike, to accelerate its digital media transformation push in the Kingdom.

GoWit will provide the technology infrastructure powering Panda’s e-commerce media platform, combining first-party data activation, AI powered auction and bidding, campaign automation, and real-time measurement and reporting.
“Panda represents the scale and ambition shaping the next phase of retail media in Saudi Arabia,” says Emrah Adsan, CEO at GoWit. “Together with Spike Media, we’re connecting advanced technology, local market demand, and omnichannel media capabilities to help Panda build a more integrated, measurable, and scalable retail media business.”

items.body:
Fashion brand SIMKHAI onboard as Croissant Pay solution expands to Shopify Checkout and in-store
Croissant, a shopping and rewards app for luxury fashion, reports that its Croissant Pay solution is now available in Shopify Checkout and at the register through Shopify POS and all other PoS systems. Fashion brand SIMKHAI is among the first to offer it through the new integration.
“Reaching a luxury customer costs more every year, and the first order rarely pays for itself. The industry needs two things: alternative means of acquiring the right shoppers, and deeper loyalty,” says John Howard, CEO and Co-Founder at Croissant.
“Croissant brings both. Our members hold spending power in Croissant: credit from the pieces they've sold, rewards from the brands they shop, and exclusive offers from the brands they want next. Croissant Pay brings that spending power to a brand's checkout and its stores, and the brand pays only when a member spends. Shoppers earn more credit on each subsequent purchase, keeping them loyal to the curated list of brands in Croissant’s network.”
SIMKHAI, a Los Angeles-based fashion house founded by Jonathan Simkhai, began accepting Croissant Pay online on 11th September, the day of its Spring/Summer 2027 runway show, and in its SoHo store on Mercer Street, where it hosted a correlating private shopping event. More than 6,600 Croissant members currently own SIMKHAI items.
“We’re continually exploring thoughtful ways to enhance the SIMKHAI customer experience,” says Martin Vestre, Chief DTC Officer at SIMKHAI. “Croissant Pay offers another way to engage with the brand while introducing SIMKHAI to a new audience.”
“Innovation has always been central to SIMKHAI, both in our design ethos and in how we connect with our customers,” adds Jonathan Simkhai. “Croissant offers a fresh way to discover us, and we’re excited to bring this partnership to our community.”

Tesco is introducing new virtual try-on technology for the first time, as part of a trial at its Sandhurst Extra store. Powered by AIUTA tech, the experience lets customers virtually try on around 1,500 items of F&F clothing across womenswear and menswear by taking a photo or uploading a photo of themselves onto a digital try-on screen in the clothing department, or selecting a digital model to view clothes in different sizes.
The trial is designed to understand how Tesco can help customers browsing in-store to discover new styles and feel more confident before they buy.
The virtual try-on screen forms part of a wider F&F refresh at Sandhurst Extra, which includes new changing rooms and a dedicated service hub for easier checking out and returns. Customers will also see a larger F&F range in-store and a refreshed look and feel with new signage, updated lighting and a focus on showcasing the F&F range across womenswear, menswear and childrenswear.

items.body:
Urgent action needed as UK retailers’ energy bills push up price of everyday essentials for shoppers
Retailers face a £440 million increase in electricity costs this year, despite their energy use remaining virtually unchanged, according to a new report from the British Retail Consortium (BRC). The trade body says it’s concerned that this will feed directly into consumer prices, raising the cost of living for millions of families.
The report notes that electricity costs are expected to rise from £2.72 billion in 2025 to £3.16 billion in 2026, an increase of 16% in just one year. Much of this rise is being driven by growing non-commodity charges (NCCs), government driven costs added to electricity bills, rather than global energy prices. These charges, which include government levies and rising and volatile network costs, now typically make up around two-thirds of retailers’ electricity bills. Transmission Network Use of System charges alone are expected to rise by 72%, adding almost £200 million to bills.
Retail is one of the UK’s major energy using industries and, following investment in decarbonisation, around 90% of the industry’s energy use now comes from electricity. This leaves retailers particularly exposed to rising electricity costs, with recent volatility in energy prices following conflict in the Middle East adding further pressure.
The increase comes as retailers face a wider squeeze from rising costs. The industry has already been hit by £6.5 billion in additional employment costs over the past two years, including higher employer national insurance contributions, above inflationary increases to the national living wage and other employment related costs.
The BRC argues that retailers have absorbed as much of these additional costs as possible to protect customers. But with margins already extremely tight, the continued rise in electricity and employment costs is making it increasingly difficult to do so without putting further pressure on prices at the till. This is particularly challenging for energy intensive parts of the industry, including food retail, where higher electricity costs risk adding to inflationary pressures at a time when household budgets remain stretched.
Helen Dickinson, Chief Executive at the British Retail Consortium, says: “Retailers’ energy bills continue to push up the price of everyday essentials for shoppers everywhere. With another £440 million increase this year despite their energy use barely changing, the Chancellor must take action to reduce the plethora of policy levies, as well as stabilise the predictability of network charges that are driving up the cost of energy. Doing so would ease pressure on retailers, giving them breathing space to invest in keeping prices down for households and keeping people in jobs.”

items.title: China’s succession crisis: a generation of entrepreneurs is retiring, but are their children ready to take over?
items.summary: Family run private businesses helped power China’s economic miracle, but the next generation is finding it difficult to carry on the work of their parents Growing up, Ayu would watch his parents put together hand made leather shoes on the ground floor of their three storey home in the Chinese city of Wenzhou. Their relatives in Europe would send photographs of designer products from Italy for the workers to base their designs on, and in the decades that followed, the tiny family-run workshop transformed into a 700 person factory. “The factory and the home were the same place. I watched them make shoes by hand, piece by piece, using small machines,” Ayu recalls of watching his parents work in the 1980’s. Continue reading...
items.body:
Growing up, Ayu would watch his parents put together hand made leather shoes on the ground floor of their three storey home in the Chinese city of Wenzhou. Their relatives in Europe would send photographs of designer products from Italy for the workers to base their designs on, and in the decades that followed, the tiny family-run workshop transformed into a 700 person factory.
“The factory and the home were the same place. I watched them make shoes by hand, piece by piece, using small machines,” Ayu recalls of watching his parents work in the 1980’s.
By the mid eighties, Chinese economists had a name for this type of bottom up economic growth story: the Wenzhou model. It was a system that saw small companies secure finances through family connections and operate underground factories to produce cheap goods that would end up on the busy streets of China and beyond.
But now many of the family-run manufacturing businesses that helped to fuel China’s economic success are facing a succession crisis, with the children of factory owners unable or unwilling to take them over.
Ayu – who today runs an online e-commerce platform – says it’s not that his generation doesn’t want to take them over, but that the market is much more competitive than when their parents started, and the crucial institutional knowledge and commercial relationships that powered their success will be impossible to pass on.
Personal relationships, experience and instincts are difficult to hand over to the next generation, says Hanqing Fang, an associate professor at Missouri University of Science and Technology.
“Shares can be passed to a son or daughter overnight,” Fang says. “But the heir is being asked to take over something that looks like a company on paper but, in practice, is closer to the founder’s personal belongings.”
“The network is very difficult to inherit,” Ayu says. “You have to build it yourself. In the end, some people inherit an empty shell. On paper they’re the boss, but the people underneath them have already begun to leave.
“We inherited the wealth, but we couldn’t inherit the industry.”
‘I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy’
According to HSBC Life research, two-thirds of wealthy Chinese people have no legacy plan. In a study led by the University of Ningbo, just 10 out of 114 private companies surveyed said they were being managed by the families’ second generation.
Many of China’s second generation business owners speak of a profound anxiety about taking over the family firm.
“I really don’t want to take over because there are so many interpersonal relationships and financial connections that I’d have to handle and learn about,” says Wu, a graduate who works in marketing in Hong Kong.
His family own a snack processing factory in the Chinese city of Shanwei, as well as dozens of stores in Shenzhen and Hong Kong. But he is reluctant to join the family business.
“Most young people dream of getting rich overnight, but I know there’s no such thing. When inheriting a fortune, you also have to consider all the complicated paperwork and whether you really have the ability to handle those responsibilities,” Wu says.
According to official estimates, China’s private sector accounts for more than half of the country’s tax revenue and 60% of its GDP. Economists say unsuccessful handovers can lead to firms losing value or even closing.
Because family-run companies represent such a large percentage of China’s private sector, if they fail in their thousands it could threaten the country’s future growth.
“The risk is not that these family firms simply disappear. It is that the capabilities embedded in the founder – including the knowhow, the supplier networks and the relationships – are lost in the handover,” Fang says.
For Wu, the idea of one day taking control of the family business is not completely out of the question, but he concedes he still has a lot to learn.
“I’d say that one day my parents’ company will be mine. But I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy,” Wu says.
“If I could just have the money without any responsibilities, I’d take it without hesitation. But the thing is, it’s not that simple.”
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei
*Given names only have been used

items.body:
The trade body has raised concern that this will feed directly into consumer prices, raising the cost of living for millions of families.
The industry report, Counting the Cost: The Growing Burden of Energy NCCs on Retail, shows electricity costs are expected to rise from £2.72bn in 2025 to £3.16bn in 2026, an increase of 16% in just one year.
Much of this rise is being driven by growing Non-Commodity Charges (NCCs) – the government-driven costs added to electricity bills, rather than global energy prices.
These charges, which include government levies and rising and volatile network costs, now typically make up around two-thirds of retailers’ electricity bills.
Transmission Network Use of System charges alone are expected to rise by 72%, adding almost £200m to bills.
Retail is one of the UK’s major energy-using industries and, following substantial investment in decarbonisation, around 90% of the industry’s energy use now comes from electricity.
This leaves retailers particularly exposed to rising electricity costs, with recent volatility in energy prices following conflict in the Middle East adding further pressure.
The increase comes as retailers face a wider squeeze from rising costs. The industry has already been hit by £6.5bn in additional employment costs over the past two years, including higher employer National Insurance contributions, above inflationary increases to the National Living Wage and other employment-related costs.
Retailers have absorbed as much of these additional costs as possible to protect customers. But with margins already extremely tight, the continued rise in electricity and employment costs is making it increasingly difficult to do so without putting further pressure on prices at the till.
This is particularly challenging for energy-intensive parts of the industry, including food retail, where higher electricity costs risk adding to inflationary pressures at a time when household budgets remain stretched.
The BRC is warning that these charges directly impact consumer prices, and has highlighted some of the steps Government could take to help ease the pressure:
- Extend eligibility for energy cost relief schemes, including future industrial competitiveness programmes, to electricity-intensive retailers.
- Remove renewable energy policy costs from electricity bills, and instead fund them centrally.
- Reform the recovery of renewable levies and system charges, to reduce pressure on electricity bills.
- Improve the predictability and stability of network charges, particularly transmission costs.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive, British Retail Consortium, said: “Retailers’ energy bills continue to push up the price of everyday essentials for shoppers everywhere.
“With another £440m increase this year despite their energy use barely changing, the chancellor must take action to reduce the plethora of policy levies, as well as stabilise the predictability of network charges that are driving up the cost of energy.
“Doing so would ease pressure on retailers, giving them breathing space to invest in keeping prices down for households and keeping people in jobs.”

items.title: After two disastrous debt-fuelled buyouts, has Boots finally found a safe haven? asks ALEX BRUMMER
items.summary: Two decades have passed since dealmaker Sir Nigel Rudd flogged off Alliance Boots to billionaire pharmacist Stefano Pessina and KKR for £11bn.
items.body:
After two disastrous debt-fuelled buyouts, has Boots finally found a safe haven? asks ALEX BRUMMER
Two decades have passed since dealmaker Sir Nigel Rudd sold High Street stalwart Alliance Boots to billionaire pharmacist Stefano Pessina and KKR for £11billion.
The sell-off was hailed as the UK’s biggest private equity buyout. It was a heady moment on the eve of the Great Financial Crisis, and a confident Pessina talked grandly of creating a global pharmacy empire stretching from Europe to the Americas and the Far East.
The journey has been far from smooth, and Boots is under fresh ownership yet again.
Instead of creating the global empire he envisaged, Pessina is like the sailor on the burning deck as another private equity partner, Sycamore, has parcelled up his empire into five different businesses and is seeking to sell them off one by one to pay down debt.
During the two-decade journey, Boots was slimmed down, the Alliance wholesale enterprise flogged, and Pessina effected a disastrous merger with American drugstore chain Walgreens.
The idea that Boots, with its health and beauty unique selling point and its successful No7 skincare and cosmetics range, would sit happily in Walgreens stores alongside the serried ranks of junk food and, at one stage, cigarettes is a fantasy.
High Street pharmacy chain Boots has been sold to Canada's billionaire Weston family in a £6.7bn deal
European retail has a long history of meeting its Gettysburg when it ventures across the Atlantic.
One supposes the remarkable thing about this sordid history for Boots, which saw its tax domicile hived off to Switzerland, is that it has remained intact.
With the help of some carefully staged investment in well-located city-centre stores, the brand and shops have survived.
But there has been little value creation and, behind the shiny facades of Piccadilly and Kensington, there is still an awfully long tail of shoddy, under-invested neighbourhood shops, good for prescriptions and toothpaste but not much else.
It remains a school for future independent chemists and an important cog in the NHS’s supply chain.
Finally, the journey looks as if it is over, with the Canadian branch of the Weston family sweeping into action with a £6.7billion deal.
The Canadian Westons are at pains to say that their Wittington ownership has nothing to do with the British branch, which controls ABF and Primark.
But they are not unknown in the UK as former owners of Selfridges and proprietors of fancy grocer Fortnum & Mason.
They are also owners of Shoppers Drug Mart, with 1,300 stores across Canada, and can claim industry expertise.
But, as Pessina discovered at Walgreens, North America is a very different market. Finally, one trusts, Boots has found a haven after a ridiculous financial odyssey.
Right royal mess
In his first stint as Business Secretary, George V doppelganger Jonathan Reynolds airily waved through a highly leveraged £3.6billion takeover of the Royal Mail owner International Distribution Services by Czech sphinx Daniel Kretinsky.
Selling a prized British asset to a billionaire who made his money from gas pipelines to Putin’s Russia was not in the public interest.
Indeed, instead of taking greater public control of a former government-owned utility, it was sold off to a foreigner backed by overseas banks.
Approving the sale, Reynolds waved a piece of paper promising to protect workers from job cuts, making a similar commitment to the unions.
Such deals are not worth the paper they are written on, and 2,500 jobs are earmarked to go by 2027. Service levels, despite a recent improvement, are still woeful.
Perhaps Prime Minister Andy Burnham should commit to adding the Royal Mail to the list of water and energy utilities he wants to see under the thumb of the state.
Never land
Labour is fantastic at making great promises and doing nothing.
The triple lock is to go, but not until the next Parliament. The Milburn review of NEETs, young people not in employment, education or training, is delayed.
Thames Water’s future is still in abeyance. Heathrow’s third runway is in doubt.
And Norway’s Equinor could do a runner unless Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh finally gives the go-ahead to drilling at the Rosebank and Jackdaw offshore oil and gas fields. Heigh-ho.

items.title: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
items.summary: The sale of the High Street chain was announced on Wednesday.
items.body:
Boots sold in Â£7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
- Published
Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (Â£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.
Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy the 177-year-old retailer on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.
Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a stalwart of the High Street, expanding its business to sell a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.
The chain has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.
Its stores have seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every weekday.
It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK in recent years, leaving it with about 1,800 stores and 51,000 employees, but remains a familiar British brand.
In its most recent annual results, Boots generated Â£7.5bn in sales - a 3.2% increase on 2024.
Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth, chief executive of savvy marketing, said shoppers were unlikely to see much change to stores in the coming months, but added what they can "expect over time is an improved shopping experience as the new owners invest in the business".
She said health and beauty was a "massive area for growth", and fresh investment from its new ownership would help.
The last two decades has seen several changes of ownership.
Sycamore only owned the retailer for 18 months, and Shuttleworth said the chopping and changing of owners had been "an unhelpful distraction".
- Boots gets new US owner in multi-billion dollar deal 
  - Published7 March 2025
The company was established by John Boot, who opened the first herbalist store in Nottingham, offering an affordable alternative to traditional medicines in 1849.
It has since expanded over the decades into selling various products, but health products have remained a key part of its business.
As well as vaccines, it offers eye and hearing tests, providing much needed health care support in everyday moments as well as at times of national crisis like the coronavirus pandemic.
It launched its loyalty scheme in 1997, the Advantage Card, which became hugely popular and a move repeated by various retailers since.
Galen Weston, the chairman of Wittington, will become chairman of Boots.
He signalled the new owners had fresh plans for the chain, including shop upgrades and an expansion of healthcare services.
"We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come," he said.
The Weston family will be buying Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. It is set be completed in early 2027.
The Weston family owns the Canadian grocery chain Loblaws, pharmacy business Shoppers Drug Mart, and previously owned the London department store Selfridges from 2003 to 2021, before selling it for $4bn.
The separate UK branch of the Weston family is the majority owner of Associated British Foods, the parent firm of Primark.
The Westons were ranked fifth on this year's Sunday Times Rich List with a combined fortune of almost Â£19bn.
Wittington will have operational control over Boots, it has secured ownership in partnership with Fairfax Financial Holdings, a Toronto-based holding company.
Sycamore Partners, in partnership with Stefano Pessina and his family, will retain ownership of The Boots Group's Farmacias Benavides in Mexico and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland in Germany.

items.title: Boots bought by Canada's billionaire Weston family for £6.7bn
items.summary: Boots confirmed it will be bought by Canada's billionaire Weston family from Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family for £6.7billion.
items.body:
Boots bought by Canada's billionaire Weston family for £6.7bn
Canada's billionaire Weston family has confirmed it has bought the Boots Group from Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family for £6.7billion.
Wittington Investments, the holding company of the Westons, said the deal included Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses.
The Westons are best-known in the UK for the Associated British Foods empire, which contains fashion chain Primark, as well as owning department store Fortnum & Mason.
The Canadian side of the family owns the grocery chain Loblaws and pharmacy chain Shoppers Drug Mart through Wittington Investments. They sold Selfridges for £4billion in 2022.
The deal has dashed all hopes of a return to the stock market after 19 years for Boots, which would have provided a much-needed boost to the City.
British chemist Boots - which began as a family herbal medicine shop in Nottingham in 1849 - has been bought by the Canadian side of the family behind Primark
Boots boss Alex Baldock, who joined last month, said 'the opportunity ahead is even greater'.
Buyout group Sycamore Partners broke up Boots’ former owner, Walgreens Boots Alliance, in August last year after its £7.4billion takeover of the US group, creating the Boots Group in the process.
Walgreens Boots Alliance boss, Italian billionaire Stefano Pessina, and his wife, Ornella Barra, continued to own a 44 per cent stake in Boots.
Pessina, who has owned Boots for two decades, said it had been 'one of the privileges of my and Ornella's life to have been so closely associated' with the pharmacy chain.
He said: 'We are delighted to be passing on a thriving Boots to strong and reliable owners who understand the value of its great heritage. Our best wishes go with them as they lead Boots into its next chapter, and our sincere thanks go to all on the Boots’ team who helped us deliver so much over the past 20 years!'
Wittington said it had partnered with Fairfax Financial Holdings, whose portfolio includes investments in the owner of Simba Sleep.
The deal does not include businesses including Mexican drugstore Farmacias Benavides and German chain Alliance Healthcare Deutschland.
Galen Weston, who will become chairman of Boots, said: ‘Boots is one of Britain’s most enduring businesses, with a rich heritage, a trusted name and a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland.’
‘We have great respect for Boots’ legacy and leading market position. We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come.’
Boots, which runs around 2,000 stores and has 51,000 staff, has been cashing in on strong beauty sales, as 'K beauty' products by popular Korean brands rise in popularity.
It is also pinning its hopes on a booming 'wellness market', including vitamin and electrolyte supplements, while the increasing uptake of weight-loss jabs has also given it a boost.
The business, which started as a family herbal medicine shop in Nottingham in 1849, last year saw annual sales rise 3.2 per cent to £7.5billion.
Danni Hewson, head of financial analysis at AJ Bell, said: 'There will be disappointment that the London market isn’t getting what could have been a high-profile new listing, particularly at a time when such additions are in short supply.
'Boots recently appointed former Currys boss Alex Baldock as CEO, seen as something as a coup thanks to Baldock’s successful recovery efforts at the electronics retailer, and he looks set to continue in the role.
'The Westons are likely to focus on making Boots run more efficiently and driving growth, potentially investing big sums to improve stores and making it more relevant for the modern age.'

items.body:
The Canadian family that once owned Selfridges department store has bought the UK pharmacy and beauty retailer Boots for $8.9bn (£6.74bn).
Wittington Investments, the holding company of the Weston family that controls the Loblaws grocery chain and Shoppers Drug Mart pharmacy outlets in Canada, will own Boots’ UK and Irish retail operations and opticians chain, the No7 beauty brand and a franchise arm in Thailand.
The acquisition of the Nottingham-headquartered chain, which has 1,800 stores across the UK and employs 50,000 people, is also being backed by the investment firm Fairfax, which owns The Sporting Life Group and Sleep Country, Canada’s largest mattress retailer, which owns Simba Sleep in the UK.
Galen Weston, the chair of Wittington, who is likely to become chair of Boots, said: “Boots is one of Britain’s most enduring businesses, with a rich heritage, a trusted name and a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland.
“We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come.”
The transaction, which sees the exit of Boots’ long-term backer Stefano Pessina and his latest backer, the financial firm Sycamore Partners, is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027.
In 2022, the US pharmacy group Walgreens put Boots up for sale with a suggested price tag of up to £10bn, but it later dropped the plans as potential buyers, including Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, the US private equity investor Apollo Global Management and Asda’s owners TDR Capital, struggled to raise funds. A plan to float the business at a valuation of about £7bn was dropped in 2024.
“Boots is an iconic brand and a British institution,” said Pessina, who took Boots private with the backing of the investment firm KKR in 2007. He has since kept a stake under different private equity owners and merged and demerged it from Walgreens.
“It has been one of the privileges of my and [my wife] Ornella’s life to have been so closely associated with Boots over the last 20 years. We are delighted to be passing on a thriving Boots to strong and reliable owners who understand the value of its great heritage.”
Pessina will retain ownership of Boots’ interests in the Farmacias Benavides pharmacy chain in Mexico and the Alliance Healthcare Deutschland, a German drug distributor.
The acquisition of Boots marks the return of the Weston family’s Canadian branch to the UK high street, after the family sold off the Selfridges department store chain for £4bn in 2022.
The separate UK branch of the family’s company is known for holding a majority stake in Primark through the parent company Associated British Foods, which is led by family member George Weston.
Richard Hyman, the veteran retail analyst, said the Weston family were “the most encouraging ownership of Boots for many, many years”.
He said: “For years, watching Boots has been a bit like watching corporate pass the parcel. Its ownership has changed with extraordinary frequency and each owner has stripped a bit more out of it.”
Hyman said Boots had an opportunity to make more of its vast loyalty scheme and to offer more services through its network of stores across the UK, many of which had seen little modernisation in recent decades.
Boots has closed more than 300 outlets in recent years. It is unclear whether its new owners plan to close more shops, but they are likely to take a close look given the rising costs of high street retail, the shift of trade to online, and competition from discounters such as Savers, Lidl and Home Bargains.
Hyman said: “Boots needs and deserves owners that will show it a bit of love, and history shows the Westons take a longer view.”

items.title: Fed voices concerns over proposed changes to vape packaging and marketing
items.summary: The Federation of Independent Retailers (the Fed) has responded to the government’s consultation on changes to vape packaging and marketing by expressing concern about the impact of certain key proposals. In particular, the Fed’s national president Hemanshu Patel highlighted misgivings about the cost and disruption… This story continues at Fed voices concerns over proposed changes to vape packaging and marketing Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
In particular, the Fed’s national president Hemanshu Patel highlighted misgivings about the cost and disruption of placing vapes behind a display screen – similar to that in place for cigarettes and tobacco.
In a letter to health secretary Yvette Cooper summarising the Fed’s response, Patel said: “Our members are local and responsible retailers. We also know our customers well and fully acknowledge concern about youth vaping.
“To that end, we already back measures to prevent children accessing vapes by proscribing under-18 access and through initiatives like Challenge 25.
“We have also been vocal supporters of recent government work to boost local authority trading standards with extra resources, as we feel this is important for enforcing effective age restrictions and for clamping down on the black market rogue trade.
“However, as our consultation response has said, we have concerns that placing vapes behind a shutter blind will limit consumer awareness and create obstacles for our shops, alongside unease about the introduction of plain vape packaging.”
Patel also expressed concern about the scope and variety of changes proposed in the large consultation and called for close engagement and sufficient preparation time for independent shops to prepare if the changes are enacted.
He called for closer engagement between the government and independent retail during a period of growing regulatory change and has offered to meet directly with the secretary of state for business Jonathan Reynolds MP, as well as Yvette Cooper, whose department led on the consultation.

items.title: One year to DRS: the return points nobody has planned for | Viewpoint: Nick Yeatman
items.summary: In twelve months the Deposit Return Scheme goes live, and the shape of the UK's return network is largely set. For the largest players it looks fairly settled. Supermarkets know what they are installing, reverse vending machine (RVM) suppliers are engaged, and the rollout across… This story continues at One year to DRS: the return points nobody has planned for | Viewpoint: Nick Yeatman Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Supermarkets know what they are installing, reverse vending machine (RVM) suppliers are engaged, and the rollout across large-format retail has a clear direction to it.
Less settled is whether the rest of the market understands what is now available to it. A significant number of convenience retailers are still planning around two options. A machine they have no room for, or a bag behind the counter – yet, a third option has arrived. That gap in awareness, more than any gap in technology, is what could hold the scheme back over the next year.
RVMs have earned their position. They are proven, high-capacity systems handling barcode verification, fraud prevention and the throughput needed for thousands of containers a day. Where a site has the floor space, the footfall and the volume, nothing serves the job better. The case for anything else does nothing to change that.
The question worth asking with a year to go is what happens at the other end of the market. More than 50,000 convenience stores, express formats and independent retailers trade across the UK, most from compact premises where every square foot has to earn its commercial keep.
A machine built for supermarket volume is the wrong fit for a shop where shelf space determines revenue directly. That is a matter of scale rather than a criticism of the technology.
This has left a large part of the sector expecting to handle returns by hand. Manual handling sounds straightforward until you run it in a small store. Staff need training on which containers qualify and which do not. Space has to be found behind the counter for bags of returns.
Someone has to manage storage, arrange collections, track what the store is owed and be confident the deposits paid out match what comes back from the scheme. For a team already running lean, that is a real operational cost, and it grows with every container returned.
There is a competitive dimension here too. Plenty of convenience retailers are wary that DRS will pull shoppers toward supermarkets, where the machine sits under the same roof as the weekly shop.
The more forward-thinking operators are starting to see it the other way round. Handled properly, container returns are a reason for someone to walk through your door, and a point of regular contact with a customer who might otherwise shop elsewhere. The appetite to take part is there. What the sector has been waiting for is a product that makes taking part straightforward.
That product now exists. A new category of semi-automated return technology sits between manual handling and the full-scale RVM.
These systems handle verification, consumer interaction and secure storage automatically, without the footprint or capital outlay of a supermarket machine. The customer scans and deposits the container themselves. The retailer does not touch it.
The important part for anyone weighing this up is that these systems connect to the scheme in the same way an RVM does. The same barcode verification. The same fraud prevention.
The same data flowing back to scheme administrators. From a compliance and reporting perspective there is no compromise, and no second-tier status. A container returned in a village shop is verified, logged and accounted for exactly as it would be in a superstore.
That connection brings practical benefits on the shop floor. Digital reporting gives real visibility of what the store is owed and when, rather than an estimate based on bags in a stockroom. Secure storage means containers stay accounted for once deposited, closing off the shrinkage and fraud risks that worry retailers about an open bag behind the counter.
A process that would otherwise depend entirely on staff becomes automated, with an audit trail behind it.
This matters well beyond the convenience channel. The success of DRS will not be decided in supermarkets alone. It depends on whether people can return containers wherever they actually live, work and shop.
Convenience stores, forecourts, neighbourhood shops, gyms, universities and leisure venues all have a part to play in building a network that works, and return rates depend on the experience being quick everywhere.
If returning a bottle at a local shop is slower and more awkward than at a supermarket, shoppers will consolidate their returns or stop bothering, and the collection figures will show it.
Consumers do not care which category of machine processes their bottle or can. They care that it takes seconds. Government cares about hitting collection targets. Retailers care about compliance, footfall and profitability. A well-designed network serves all three by matching the right technology to the right site rather than applying a single template everywhere.
With a year to go, the task for the industry is not to choose between manual and automated. RVMs will keep doing what they do well in the sites built for them. The work still to be done is awareness. Tens of thousands of retailers who fall between the two existing options now have a third, and twelve months to plan around it.
Nick Yeatman is CEO and founder of Trovr

items.title: Mike Ashley’s Frasers builds stakes in Burberry and Under Armour
items.summary: Frasers Group, the retail empire founded by Mike Ashley, has taken a stake in athleisure giant Under Armour and built up its holding in fashion house Burberry. The London-listed conglomerate, which owns Sports Direct and Flannels, has pushed up its position in the FTSE 100 fashion brand from 4.2 to 6.3 per cent of the [...]
items.body:
Mike Ashley’s Frasers builds stakes in Burberry and Under Armour
Frasers Group, the retail empire founded by Mike Ashley, has taken a stake in athleisure giant Under Armour and built up its holding in fashion house Burberry.
The London-listed conglomerate, which owns Sports Direct and Flannels, has pushed up its position in the FTSE 100 fashion brand from 4.2 to 6.3 per cent of the company.
These shares are held through put options, meaning that Frasers does not yet own this stake but has the right to buy it at a fixed price.
Mike Ashley’s retail group has tightened its grip on the UK’s biggest luxury designer just days after it signalled plans to expand further into up-market clothing.
On Monday, the company unveiled Frasers Group Luxury – a new arm of the firm encompassing Flannels, department store chains Harvey Nichols and The Webster, as well as its investments in Burberry and bagmaker Mulberry.
Chief executive Michael Murray, Ashley’s son-in-law, said the group hopes to widen its presence in luxury fashion through “organic expansion, acquisitions, and strategic investments”.
The statement of intent was welcomed by Burberry chief executive Joshua Schulman, who praised Frasers’ “deep understanding of their customers” and its ability to offer up-market fashion to shoppers in regional cities like Leeds and Liverpool, where it has flagship Flannels stores.
Schulman, who joined Burberry in 2024, is beginning to make progress in his turnaround of the fashion house, which has pivoted towards “timeless British luxury” in its bid to appeal to more shoppers.
Frasers keeps one toe in sportswear
Despite Frasers Group’s up-market ambitions, Mike Ashley appears unlikely to abandon the sportswear market which kickstarted his career in retail.
Frasers, which was founded as Sports Direct in 1982, has bought an 8.8 per cent stake in Under Armour, the American sportswear brand.
Ashley’s firm has bought about 16.6m shares in the athleisure group, according to a US filing, worth about $80m.
Under Armour chief executive Kevin Plank welcomed Frasers’ shareholding, telling business newspaper Footwear News: “We value their support and remain focused on executing our strategy and creating long-term value for all shareholders.
“We look forward to building on our relationship with Frasers as both a shareholder and an important commercial partner.”
Plank is seeking to push the sportswear brand upmarket as it hunts for a turnaround. The group’s sales slipped by three per cent to $1.1bn (£830m) in the three months to June.
Frasers Group also holds shares in athletic giant Puma, and owns a number of sports brands including Slazenger, Everlast, Lonsdale and Karrimor.
Shares in Frasers rose by more than three per cent on Wednesday, to 846p. The stock has gained 26 per cent in the year to date.

Having fell short of the target, Co-op Wholesale… This story continues at Co-op Wholesale discontinues delivery app Peckish in favour of Snappy Shopper Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The Peckish app initially launched in February 2025 with a goal to sign up 1,000 independent stores. Having fell short of the target, Co-op Wholesale has decided to switch its focus to Snappy Shopper via Co-op’s Evolution EPoS till system.
Retailers will also be able to handle orders from other major platforms like Deliveroo, Just Eat, and Uber Eats through a single order aggregation tool.
Katie Secretan, Co-op Wholesale managing director, commented: “We’re progressing through the year well and having to make decisions that are right by the business and right by our retailers, and this is one of those.
“Our primary focus is on supporting our retailers where they need it most and providing the best services to them that can help grow their business. This is why we’re doubling down with Snappy.
“We see their technology as leading for home delivery for independent retailers and are excited about expanding the relationship including releasing the direct EPOS integration with Evolution making it even easier for retailers to trade on platforms such as Snappy Shopper, Deliveroo, Uber Eats and Just Eat.”
“We are simplifying our quick commerce proposition by transitioning Peckish retailers onto an established and proven delivery platform, Snappy Shopper. This decision supports our retailers, who we are providing with access to a larger customer base and more mature delivery ecosystem in a single strategic quick commerce partner.”

items.title: We've tracked prices on 20 major Prime Day deals to see whether shoppers should buy now or wait until Black Friday
items.summary: We tracked prices on 20 major Prime Day deals over the past six months, to check if they are genuine discounts or have been sold at a cheaper price in the past.
items.body:
We've tracked prices on 20 major Prime Day deals to see whether shoppers should buy now or wait until Black Friday
Products featured in this article are independently selected by This is Money's specialist journalists. If you open an account using links which have an asterisk, This is Money will earn an affiliate commission. We do not allow this to affect our editorial independence.
Amazon Prime Big Deal Days have arrived for 48 hours only.
Offers are being advertised on everything from smart home gadgets and tech to kitchen appliances, vacuums, and top-rated beauty products.
But should we be filling our baskets, or is it better to wait for Black Friday on November 27 to get the best deals?
We tracked prices on 20 major Prime Day deals over the past six months, to check if they are genuine discounts or have been sold at a cheaper price in the past.
We reveal the current asking price, what it previously sold for, it's price fluctuation over the past six months, and whether you should buy it now or wait.
Amazon Prime Day Deals: Some of the offers look tempting, but should you buy now or wait until Black Friday?
Tech
Was £1,299
One of the top deals right now is the Hisense 55 inch miniLED TV (55Q8STUK). Over the past six months, this model typically hovered around £650 to £799 outside sales.
The £1,299 original list price is inflated, but its price drop to £529 is a true six-month low.
Verdict? Buy now.
Data shows TV discounts during October Prime sales rarely improve by more than £10 to £20 on Black Friday, and stock often runs low.
The Ring Battery Video Doorbell & Indoor Camera Bundle is currently £39.99, marked down from £119.98.
These device bundles usually fluctuate between £69.99 and £119.98 during non-sale periods. A price of £39.99 for both items is an all-time low.
Verdict? Buy now.
Ring is owned by Amazon, and its tech products tend to hit their maximum discounts during October Prime Big Deal Days. Black Friday will match, but not beat, this price.
Was £79.99
The Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K is currently £34.99. It was £79.99.
Its normal price is £59.99, but it drops to £34.99 to £39.99 during major clearance events.
Verdict? Buy now.
Amazon usually discounts the 4K Stick to around this price again on Black Friday, but it isn't likely to go any lower.
Was £159.89
The newest generation of the Echo Dot smart speaker, which comes in a pack of two, is currently £56.98.
Previously £159.98, the cost has been slashed by 64 per cent.
While single units regularly sell for £29.99 to £54.99 each, a two-pack deal effectively drops individual units to under £28.50.
Verdict? Buy Now.
Echo hardware is matching its bottom-tier Black Friday price right now.
The Soundcore Anker P30i Wireless Earbuds are just £22.79. They usually sell for double the price at £49.99.
The price averaged between £29.99 and £39.99 across spring and summer 2026. £22.79 is near its lowest historic price.
Verdict? Buy now.
Small-ticket audio gear hits its floor around £20 to £23. Black Friday won't yield meaningful extra savings.
Cleaning
Was £319.99.
The Shark Corded Upright Vacuum (NZ691UKTDB) is currently £295.95. Usually they sell for around £319.99.
However, Shark uprights fluctuate wildly between £149 and £220 over a six-month window depending on weekly voucher codes.
Verdict? Wait.
We think you should hold out for Black Friday when shark models consistently drop to around £139.
Was £139.99.
The Eufy Robot Vacuum Cleaner G50 is now £88.82. It was £139.99.
While it has settled around £110 to £139 over the last six months, a price of under £90 is a rare flash-deal floor.
Verdict? Buy now.
Entry-level Eufy robot vacuums rarely drop below £85. Grab it while in stock.
Was £174.99
The Shark StainForce Cordless Spot Cleaner is currently £99.99, marked down from £174.99.
It has hovered around £130 to £150 since its release earlier this year. Sub-£100 is its lowest recorded point.
Verdict? Buy now.
We think £99.99 is a target threshold for spot cleaners. Black Friday is unlikely to go lower.
Was £99.99
The Philips OneUp 3000 Series Electric Mop is on sale for £69.99, down from £99.99.
Fluctuation has been minor, typically selling between £89 and £109 over the past six months.
Verdict? Wait.
Floor-care appliances see heavier competition and deeper cuts in late November.
The Shark VacMop 2-in-1 Cordless Spray Mop (VM200UK) is currently £55.99.
It was £99.99, marked down by 44 per cent.
Retailed between £70 and £99 over the last six months. £55.99 is a current bottom-level deal.
Verdict? Buy now.
This is a solid price for a daily hard-floor cleaner.
Kitchen
Was £229.99
The Ninja MAX Dual Zone Digital Air Fryer 9.5L is selling for £161.45. It previously sold for £229.99.
It averaged £179 – £199 during summer 2026, occasionally hitting £169.
Verdict? Buy now.
The current asking price is highly reasonable for the 9.5L model. Black Friday may match it, but stock risks selling out fast.
Was £19.99
Hejo’s four Pack Ice Cream Tubs for Ninja CREAMi are selling for £15.99, once £19.99.
They remained static at £18.99 to £19.99 through the summer peak season.
Verdict? Buy now.
Third-party accessories rarely receive deeper cuts than 20 per cent regardless of the sale event.
Was £114.99
PHILIPS L'OR Barista Sublime Pod Machine is currently £51.29. It usually sells for double the price at £114.99.
This coffee machine typically sits around £69.99 to £89.99; RRP is inflated, but £51.29 is still a strong six-month low.
Verdict? Buy now.
Entry-level pod machines rarely drop below £50.
Beauty
Was £16.90
Medicube’s Toner Pads Zero Pore Pad 2.0 are selling for just £11.50, previously £16.90.
The price fluctuated between £14.50 and £16.90 over the past six months.
Verdict? Buy now.
K-Beauty items on Amazon hit peak discounts during Prime events; Black Friday usually mirrors these exact prices.
We also have the Medicube PDRN Collagen Gua Sha Neck Wrinkle Cream (90ml).
This is selling for £20, marked down from £29.99.
Since launching, this viral built-in applicator cream has stayed near its standard list price of £32 to £36 across UK importers and Amazon, rarely dipping below £28.
Verdict? Buy now.
Prime Day offers on viral K-Beauty devices/hybrids hit peak discounts (around 30 to 35 per cent off). Black Friday will likely match this rate rather than beat it.
Was £59.99
The Revolution Pro Miracle LED Face Mask is currently £40. It was £59.99.
The price has held steady at around £49.99 to £59.99 since launching earlier this year.
Verdict? Buy now.
At £40, it reaches standard budget-LED promo pricing.
The Oral-B iO2 Electric Toothbrush (with Travel Case) is selling for £37.99. Its RRP is £100.
An RRP of £100 is a promotional anchor price, while its average six-month selling price was £45 to £55.
Verdict? Buy now.
Sub-£40 for an iO series brush with a travel case is an absolute floor price.
Household
Was £50
Finish Dishwasher Tablets (166 Count) are selling for £20.69. They were priced at £50.
Price-wise they fluctuated between £24 and £32 over the past six months. Meanwhile the £50 RRP is non-functional bulk anchor pricing.
Verdict? Buy now.
Bulk household essentials hit their absolute lowest cost-per-unit during Amazon Prime events. Stock up now.
Was £8.50
Velvet Classic Quilted Toilet Tissue (24 Rolls) are selling for £7.22. Its RRP is £8.50.
Looking at its price history, it has hovered around £7.50 to £8.50 across supermarkets and Amazon over the last six months.
Verdict? Wait.
If you’re looking to buy in bulk, consider holding off until Black Friday. The 15 per cent off staple is a basic supermarket match rather than a true doorbuster deal.
Was £26.50
Bold Laundry Detergent PODS (100 Count) is selling for £19.31. Its RRP is £26.50.
This product was consistently sold between £22 and £26 in bulk over the last six months (~19p/pod).
Verdict? Buy now.
Under 20p per pod for name-brand laundry detergent is a Prime-exclusive bulk clearance rate.
Was £29.99
Duracell Plus AA Alkaline Batteries (36-Pack) are selling for £24.99. They were previously £29.99.
Consistently priced around £28 to £30 over the past six months. Bulk battery deals on Prime events represent the primary window for lower cost-per-unit.
Verdict? Buy now.
Household staples rarely drop further for Black Friday. Good time to stock up ahead of holiday gift usage.

items.body:
Boots is recruiting for thousands of new seasonal roles in its stores, warehouses and customer service centre, creating exciting employment opportunities this festive period.
As Boots prepares for its busiest time of the year, candidates of all ages will be welcome to apply for these flexible and part-time roles, including young people and first-time jobseekers – who typically make up around half of seasonal recruits at Boots.
Around 6,000 seasonal roles are available nationwide, across the retailer’s 1,800 stores, support office and warehouses, including:
- Customer Advisors and Operations Assistants, ensuring customers receive the excellent experience and expert in-store advice that they expect from Boots
- Warehouse Operatives and Picker Packers who play a crucial role in the smooth running of the supply chain, helping to keep shelves full and online orders processed.
- Roles in the Boots Customer Support Centre, supporting customers with their queries during the busy festive season
The roles are open to a wide-range of job-seekers and reflect the variety of ways that Boots customers can shop at Boots this festive season. This includes in- store roles which support customers shopping online via boots.com, through Click & Collect and via on-demand delivery partners UberEats, Just Eat and Deliveroo.
Donna Hodgins, director of talent acquisition at Boots, said: “For many people, the festive season can be the perfect opportunity to gain valuable workplace experience, build confidence and develop skills that will support them throughout their careers. Colleagues who join us over this period become an integral part of our team during one of the most exciting times of the year for retail. These roles provide hands-on experience in customer service, operations and teamwork, and for many people can be the first step on a longer-term career journey with Boots.”
Seasonal colleagues at Boots will benefit from a competitive hourly rate, Boots colleague discount and access to a wide range of benefits, including savings on cinema tickets, holidays and more.
Roles are now open to apply for online. To apply for an in-store Christmas Customer Advisor role today, visit boots.jobs/christmas. For Customer Support Centre Roles, visit boots.jobs/support-office/customer-support-centre. For distribution centre roles, visit boots.jobs/supply-chain/warehouse

items.body:
Leeds-based halal food brand Ayah Halal is bringing authentic chicken pakora to shoppers, with its Speciality Chicken Pakora set to become available at Abu Bakr Supermarket.
Made with fresh halal chicken and an authentic blend of spices and ingredients, the new ready-to-cook product has been created to give customers the taste of traditional chicken pakora at home, without the need for lengthy preparation.
Priced at £6.99 per pack, Ayah Halal’s Speciality Chicken Pakora is freshly prepared and ready to cook, giving families a convenient way to enjoy authentic, restaurant-style pakora as part of a meal, snack or sharing platter.
The chicken is coated in Ayah Halal’s signature blend before being freshly prepared, creating a flavoursome and crispy pakora while keeping the chicken tender and juicy inside.
Customers will also be able to choose their preferred spice level, making the product suitable for those who enjoy a milder flavour as well as those who prefer their pakora with an extra kick.
The Speciality Chicken Pakora can be fried or air fried, making it a convenient option for busy families who want to enjoy authentic halal food at home.
The product will now be available at Abu Bakr Supermarket, giving shoppers the opportunity to pick up Ayah Halal’s authentic chicken pakora as part of their regular grocery shop.
Hamza Hussain, Managing Director of Abu Bakr Supermarket, said the supermarket was pleased to be bringing the product to its customers.
“Chicken pakora is a firm favourite with our customers, and we’re delighted to be making this authentic product available at Abu Bakr Supermarket.
“We know our customers are looking for high-quality halal products that are convenient to prepare at home, and Ayah Halal’s Speciality Chicken Pakora offers exactly that.
“It has been carefully prepared with authentic flavours and quality ingredients, and we’re looking forward to seeing our customers enjoy it.”
The Speciality Chicken Pakora forms part of Ayah Halal’s growing range of ready-to-cook products, combining authentic flavours with the convenience of food that is prepared and ready to cook at home.
Ayah Halal has developed a range of fresh halal meat, marinated products and ready-to-cook meals, giving customers convenient options for family meals, snacks and entertaining.
The launch at Abu Bakr Supermarket will make the Speciality Chicken Pakora more accessible to shoppers looking for an authentic halal food option that can be prepared quickly at home.
With chicken pakora remaining a popular choice for family meals, gatherings and evening snacks, Ayah Halal’s new product offers customers a convenient way to enjoy an authentic taste without having to prepare the chicken and spices themselves.
The Speciality Chicken Pakora will be available at Abu Bakr Supermarket and through Ayah Halal online.

items.body:
Lidl GB has today announced its latest investment in lower prices for customers in the run-up to Christmas, demonstrating its commitment to delivering unbeatable value for British households.
The discounter has invested £400 million in price cuts and promotions across more than 1,200 products so far this year – with customers seeing prices drop on everyday staples including seasonal fruit and veg, meat and fish.
On top of market leading pricing, Lidl is also investing an additional £75 million in customer savings via Lidl Plus between now and Christmas. This includes £50 million in loyalty initiatives – such as personalised coupons and Lidl Points so customers can get offers on more of what they really value – alongside £25 million in targeted food and “Middle of Lidl” offers.
As shoppers seek more flexible ways to save, over five million Lidl Plus Marketplace coupons were redeemed this summer and Lidl Plus transactions were up 17% last month, highlighting the growing demand for personalised rewards. The discounter has boosted funding for personalised coupons by 60% this year and introduced new initiatives such as Lidl Plus Points – which gives customers the freedom to decide when and what they use their Points on. Running this week, Lidl Plus users are able to bag 10 times the usual Lidl Points on the discounter’s premium Deluxe products from 1st to 14th October.
Richard Bourns, Chief Commercial Officer at Lidl GB, commented: “Our momentum provides us with the scale to keep doing what we do best: reinvesting directly back into the pockets of British households and delivering unbeatable value across the board.
“With household budgets tight and many feeling the pinch in the run up to Christmas, we’ve cut prices across more than 1,200 products this year. It’s proof of our commitment to unbeatable value, ensuring customers never have to compromise on quality or freshness.”
Alongside lower prices, Lidl is continuously enhancing the in-store experience through technology designed to make shopping faster and easier. This includes the rollout of its Lidl & Go mobile self-scanning solution via the Lidl Plus app, AI-enabled smart scales that automatically detect produce for effortless weighing, and expanded Self-Service Checkouts (SCOs) to offer friction-free payment options for every basket size.
These latest price cuts follow on from Lidl GB’s FY25 financial results published earlier this week, where it revealed it welcomed an additional 43 million customer visits last year thanks to strategic investments in price, store expansion and digital innovation.
Higher customer footfall drove a 486 million product volume increase and 10.8% turnover increase, while the supermarket experienced over £650 million in direct switching from competitors. Lidl is stepping up its expansion to bring its low prices to even more locations, opening more than 50 new stores this financial year.

items.body:
GenM, the Menopause Partner for brands and home of the MTick – the universal shopping symbol and certification for menopause-friendly products, is taking over the UK high street with the unveiling of the world’s first dedicated menopause concept store, designed to showcase what the future of menopause retail could look like.
There are approximately 15.5million perimenopausal and menopausal women in the UK, representing a £2.4billion annual spend in the health and beauty category alone. However, GenM research reveals that 87% of menopausal women feel overlooked and underserved by brands, 66% struggle to find the products that support them, and 45% feel invisible, lonely and dispensable. Significantly, 94% of menopausal women in the UK want to shop ‘menopause-friendly’ labelled products and 96% of women told GenM they want a one-stop destination for menopause shopping, highlighting a clear demand for better product visibility, accessibility, inclusivity and trust.
GenM’s world-first menopause concept store is taking the bold first step in closing this gap, showcasing what a menopause-friendly retail space on the high street could look like and giving brands a new way to engage with this significant yet currently underserved consumer market.
Located on Kensington High Street and in collaboration with raye the store, the limited‑time concept store will be open to the public from 1st to 11th October 2026. Every element of the space has been designed with the needs of the menopausal shopper in mind, with expert advice from GP Dr Megha Dhavale – from ambient temperatures of 21°C and soft lighting to calming music and soothing scents, and clear educational signage to help women recognise and understand the 48 signs of menopause.
Every step towards a more inclusive retail landscape is thanks to the commitment of the GenM collective: over 170 of the most progressive, purposeful brands and retailers, united by the MTick to better understand, support and serve the menopausal consumer. This latest step, the menopause-friendly concept store, is supported by its Lead Campaign Partners: L’Oreal, E45, Pharmacy2U, Sainsbury’s and Tesco, Campaign Partner LoveHoney, and a significant list of supporting brands, from Cloud Nine to Sanex.
At the heart of this campaign is the MTick, the trusted, universal shopping symbol and certification for menopause-friendly products. The MTick gives consumers a simple way to identify products that have met rigorous criteria for supporting menopause, while giving brands a credible way to demonstrate their commitment to this significant consumer demographic. Everything in the GenM store carries the MTick certification, encouraging shoppers to “Know the sign. Look for the MTick.”
By bringing trusted information, expert guidance and menopause-friendly products together under one roof, GenM is making it easier for women to search, source and shop with confidence. Choice and customer journey go hand-in-hand, which is why products in the concept store span a wide range of categories, including skincare, haircare, nutrition, femtech, food and drink, bedding, and clothing, speaking to the vast 48 signs of menopause. More than just a pop-up, the concept is designed to demonstrate a new retail model for menopause that puts women’s needs at the heart of the shopping experience while creating a valuable new route for brands to reach, engage and support the 15.5 million customers within this forever market.
GenM research found that 96% of women see the MTick as a symbol of trust, demonstrating the value of clear, credible signposting at the point of purchase and highlighting the opportunity for brands to build recognition and trust with menopausal consumers. For brands, the MTick offers more than a certification mark. It provides a way to differentiate, demonstrate credibility and make their products easier for menopausal consumers to identify and discover in an increasingly significant market. With leading brands and retailers already embracing the MTick, GenM is inviting more businesses to join the movement and help shape the future of menopause retail.
Heather Jackson, CEO and co-founder of GenM, comments: “When I founded GenM seven years ago, it was because I wanted something I couldn’t find for myself: somewhere I could easily search, source and shop for products that could support me through my menopause journey.
“My original idea was to create a one-stop shop destination for menopause-friendly support. But retail wasn’t yet ready to recognise the role it could play in serving women like me better. But that idea stayed with me. It became the catalyst for the MTick, and a much bigger purpose: to normalise the menopause conversation, break the taboo, and change the rhetoric from fear to thrive.
“Today, more than 4,000 products have earned their MTick certification, and seeing a selection of them brought together here in an accessible, inclusive and vibrant pop-up retail environment on Kensington High Street feels like a very proud full-circle moment. This isn’t about curing menopause, but making the lived experience better, starting with how we shop. I hope this pop-up becomes a catalyst for a much bigger change, where dedicated menopause spaces are no longer a world-first, but an expected part of the retail shopping experience, both in-store and online. This wasn’t there for me when I needed it. But it is here for you now, and it will be even better for our future daughters.”
To support those experiencing hygiene poverty, GenM has also partnered with national charity, Beauty Banks. 10% of sales from every purchase will support the charity, and any leftover stock will be donated to help people across the UK access essential hygiene and personal care products, supporting wellbeing, dignity and confidence.
GenM’s world’s first menopause-friendly store, in collaboration with raye the store, is located at 96 Kensington High Street, London, W8 4SG and is open to the general public between 1st-11th October 2026. Opening hours: Monday – Saturday: 10 am-7 pm, Sunday: 12 pm-6 pm.

items.body:
As consumers continue to invest in advanced facial skincare, a new beauty retail category is having its moment: hand care. Once considered an afterthought, hands are now being recognised as a key indicator of skin health, with demand for targeted, high-performance formulas continuing to grow.
With winter approaching, there’s no better time to spotlight the hand creams set to become beauty bag essentials.
Shalin Balasuriya, co-founder of Spa Ceylon, wellness expert and certified sound healer, comments on why hands have become a focal point: “It comes down to visibility – and what that visibility reveals.
Hands are consistently exposed yet historically overlooked in skincare routines. As consumers have become more invested in facial skincare, the contrast is becoming harder to ignore. In many cases, hands are one of the first areas where signs of ageing appear – through changes in texture, tone and overall skin quality – making that gap even more noticeable.
There’s also a functional reality. Frequent washing, sanitising, and environmental exposure weaken the skin barrier over time, accelerating visible damage.
What’s changing now is awareness. Hands are no longer treated as an afterthought, but as an extension of overall skin health – requiring the same level of care, consistency, and formulation as the face.”
To celebrate the rise of hand care, we’ve rounded up the winter must-haves across our clients:
Spa Ceylon Cardamom Rose Intensive Hand Cream, Tal MED Hand Cream Repair and Oriflame Love Potion Cherry On Top Hand Cream. All feature nourishing formulas designed to restore hydration, protect the skin barrier, and keep hands looking their best throughout the colder months.
