items.title: Could an exit from Europe bolster Tesco’s UK dominance?
items.summary: Like a student nearing the end of their gap year, Tesco has careened across Europe, Asia, even the United States, and is now preparing to return home and settle down.  The supermarket chain, the UK’s largest, is weighing up whether to offload its operations in Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, with grocery rival Lidl [...]
items.body:
Could an exit from Europe bolster Tesco’s UK dominance?
Like a student nearing the end of their gap year, Tesco has careened across Europe, Asia, even the United States, and is now preparing to return home and settle down.
The supermarket chain, the UK’s largest, is weighing up whether to offload its operations in Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, with grocery rival Lidl among the interested parties.
This retreat from Europe, which Tesco could confirm when it updates shareholders on Thursday, would bring to an end the grocer’s globetrotting expansion and spell nothing but trouble for its British competitors.
Back in 2007, there was no land the supermarket chain did not think it could conquer. Sir Terry Leahy, who had then been Tesco’s chief executive for a decade, hailed the retailer’s expansion into the US as just one part of a “pretty ambitious” play for global dominance.
The supermarket hoped to generate more than half of its annual revenue from overseas markets within the following decade, nearly double the 27 per cent it achieved at the time.
“We keep looking at everywhere,” Sir Terry told The Times, naming India and even Russia as potential targets. “We are on the threshold of becoming one of the few successful international retailers. There’s plenty to do.”
Fast forward nearly 20 years, and there’s little still to do. With its “central” European operations on the chopping block, Tesco has already withdrawn from France, Japan, Malaysia, Poland, South Korea, Thailand, Turkey and America.
The supermarket quit its US experiment in 2013, selling off all remaining Fresh & Easy stores, and the accounting scandal that nearly sunk the firm accelerated its turn inwards in 2014. Tesco’s Thai and Malaysian operations were sold for £8bn in 2020.
The group’s European division accounted for £4.5bn of its £66.6bn total revenue last year and was recently described by chief executive Ken Murphy as an “integral part of the group”. But the UK’s biggest grocer looks prepared to cut its losses.
European exit ‘logical’ for Tesco
Shareholders would be unlikely to shed any tears if Tesco confirmed this move later this week, analysts said. The supermarket is riding high in the UK, with a market share more than 10 per cent clear of its closest rival, Sainsbury’s.
Nicholas Found, an analyst at Retail Economics, told City AM that a sale of Tesco’s European operations would have “strategic logic at the right price”. “A disposal would simplify the group, sharpen management focus and free up capital for the UK and Ireland, where the potential returns are likely to be greater,” he said.
“The danger is selling a good asset too cheaply. Tesco has no pressing need to exit, so Ken Murphy can afford to be highly disciplined on valuation.”
Though Sainsbury’s appears rock solid in second place by market share, Tesco’s renewed focus on the UK could cause alarm for Asda and Morrisons, who have both struggled with hefty debt piles following private equity takeovers.
Investors will nonetheless hope to see renewed proof that Tesco is adding to its towering market share. The grocer’s shares slipped three per cent in one day in July, when the company revealed sales growth had slowed to just one per cent.
Market share softens
Analysts have blamed Tesco’s recent lack of market share gains on the recoveries of Marks & Spencer Food and Co-op, which were both flailing in the wake of cyber attacks at this time last year.
Tesco’s market share dipped from 28.1 to 27.8 per cent in the three months to September, according to recent figures from Worldpanel by Numerator. Though an improvement from its low of 25.6 per cent in 2020, Tesco’s market share today is far from its 2007 heyday, when it accounted for nearly £1 in every £3 spent at the checkout tills.
Tesco boss Murphy could send investors a further signal of its commitment to the UK market if it confirms its interest in Majestic Wines. Tesco is reportedly weighing up a swoop for the wine retailer, in what would be its first takeover move since it bought wholesaler Booker for £3.7bn in 2017.
Independent retail analyst Richard Hyman said a disposal of Tesco’s European business “clearly makes sense. The gradual divestment of its overseas businesses has allowed it to fully focus on the core domestic business.
“Interestingly, more recent market share has been surprisingly brittle. My view is this is a small blip but they need to reassure [investors] on this and how and why it’s going to return to positive territory soon.”

items.title: Australian consumer confidence plunges to worst level since 1990s after RBA rate rise
items.summary: Key indicator dropped about 20% after the Reserve Bank last month announced the highest interest rates since 2011 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian households are the most persistently pessimistic they have been since the early-1990s recession, after a fourth rate rise this year. Confidence among Australian consumers has plunged about 20% since the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted interest rates to the highest levels since 2011, according to the Westpac–Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index. Continue reading...
items.body:
Australian households are the most persistently pessimistic they have been since the early-1990s recession, after a fourth rate rise this year.
Confidence among Australian consumers has plunged about 20% since the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted interest rates to the highest levels since 2011, according to the Westpac–Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index.
The survey, conducted between 28 September and 1 October, showed the confidence index dropped by 4.7% to 80.4% in October – the worst level since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict in early April.
But for respondents surveyed after the RBA call on 29 September, the index dropped to 67.2% – the lowest level since the late 1990s.
That was broadly in line with the weekly ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer survey, which fell about 5% to 67.1 points.
Westpac’s head of Australian macro-forecasting, Matthew Hassan, said sentiment had been extremely weak for the longest period since the “disastrous” recession of the early 1990s.
“Australian consumers remain stuck in a cost-of-living nightmare that seems to have no end in sight,” Hassan said.
“The latest RBA move looks to have badly rattled consumers. Responses over the course of the survey week show a very sharp deterioration after the decision was announced.”
Assessments of family finances and buyer sentiment were the biggest categories affected.
Expectations about the economic outlook fell less sharply, but assessments about the economy in the next five years were back to lows not seen since August 2020, shortly after Melbourne’s second lockdown and before jobkeeper subsidies were expanded.
AMP economist My Bui said the decline was unsurprising given the September rate hike and rising fuel prices.
“On our calculation the weekly petrol bill for a typical Australian household has gone up by $20 versus the beginning of the year,” Bui said.
“The worry with declining confidence is that it tends to correlate with household spending on a per capita basis: the downtrend in confidence over the past 12 months suggests consumption per person will likely fall further into contraction this year.”
Mortgage holders were the most pessimistic home ownership subgroup given rising borrowing costs at 77 index points.
Those who own their home outright experienced the largest decline in sentiment in the month, as the housing market downturn extended for a sixth month.
Renters were the most optimistic, unchanged at 84.8 points.
Hassan said fears of job losses were rising, with unemployment expectations ticking up 1.9% higher. But there are still signs the labour market is holding strong.
Citi analysts Josh Williamson and Faraz Syed said “job vacancies have increased to a two-year high of 122 points, which accords with business sentiment expectations of positive employment growth”.

items.title: Last call for the mall? How shopping centres are reinventing themselves
items.summary: In the internet age, medium-sized retail hubs are looking for new ways to survive and thrive.
items.body:
Last call for the mall? How shopping centres are reinventing themselves
- Published
The Brunel Centre was once a thriving retail destination, attracting shoppers from far and wide.
"It was incredible," says town councillor Keith Ely, who remembers its opening in Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, in 1973.
Back then, centre:MK, a large destination shopping centre four miles away in Milton Keynes, did not exist, and the Brunel was quite the draw.
Now, like many other medium-sized shopping centres, it is struggling.
Vacant units and graffiti-daubed shutters dominate, and it has just one store left.
That remaining shop, a Boots Opticians, is set to close later this month ahead of the centre's planned demolition next year.
But Ely, 87, is not upset to see the Brunel make way for flats and a health centre, with only some retail space.
"It is a sad old building, isn't it?" he says. "There is no nostalgia from me."
In the Grafton Centre, Cambridge, it is a similar story, with shuttered units, a large empty former Debenhams department store and a permanently closed cinema.
There are long-term plans for a redevelopment to include retail but also a life science centre.
This may work in Cambridge, a global leader in life sciences, but it is not an option in much of the country.
So, in the age of online shopping, what lies ahead for these medium-sized malls?
"There are too many in the UK and many don't have a future," is the stark assessment of Subjit Jassy, a director at Pioneer Group, which owns the centre.
"The old model of retailers expanding to improve turnover has now disappeared because of the internet."
1 of 4
Analysis by commercial property firm CBRE, external found that while the vacancy rate across UK shopping centres in the second quarter of this year was 16%, it was "significantly lower" at major centres.
Meanwhile, research by estate agents Savills found between April and June 2026 almost 73% of consumer spending in shopping centres was in the biggest sites, with less than 18% in secondary, or medium-sized centres.
"It is not just that shopping centres have one destiny; they really don't," says Dr Kardi Somerfield, a lecturer in marketing at the University of Northampton.
Some destination shopping centres are running at "almost 100% occupancy", she adds.
Back at the Brunel, Labour's Ed Hume, responsible for housing at Milton Keynes City Council, says: "We do need shops.
"The change here is about making sure we have a town centre that is much more open."
The hope is that more town centre homes will increase the number of people to use local businesses.
Similar plans in Norwich will see the Anglia Square development primarily replaced by housing.
But there are other options rather than just tearing a centre down.
Market Walk in Northampton is to become a leisure and entertainment space.
"Other shopping centres have a really important purpose as a community hub," says Somerfield, outlining another potential use.
This is what management are trying to achieve at another site that opened in the 1970s: Weston Favell, on the eastern edge of Northampton.
Footfall â the number of customers entering the building â has increased every year since the pandemic, says centre manager Kevin Legg.
"We are still relevant today," he says.
"Other shopping centres are trying to emulate and create what we've got."
What they have got is a mix of a large supermarket, a number of big national brands and smaller independent businesses, as well as other community facilities.
Not far from the library inside the centre is a church. It is currently being used by Silhouette Youth Theatre, a charity that aims to make the arts more accessible.
Next year it plans to create a 250-seat theatre inside part of a former Wilko store.
George Grande, voice lead at Silhouette, says being located in a shopping centre means more people can easily arrive by public transport and gives the group more visibility.
"We've had it before where people are like 'Oh, what's this? We don't know what this is.'
"That is how we can get other people to join us."

items.title: Community supermarket opens in shopping centre
items.summary: Shoppers can access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries at the new social supermarket.
items.body:
Community supermarket opens in shopping centre
- Published
A new community supermarket offering access to affordable and healthy food has opened in a Kent shopping centre.
The store run by SEK Community Food Shop welcomed the public to its home on the first floor of The Pentagon Centre in Chatham.
Gina English from SEK says the shop is open to all as "in addition to supporting people with food insecurity, people will also be able get wraparound support from us, help with employment, looking at CVs and interview skills. We're also going to help people with budgeting and money management and signposting to other local services".
Initial funding to set up the supermarket was provided by Medway Council through the Crisis and Resilience Fund.
Shoppers can walk straight into the social supermarket, with no prior booking required, to access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries, including a Â£1 fruit and vegetable bag.
Cost are kept low as the store redistributes surplus food to reduce waste, helping to protect the environment at the same time.
SEK already operates two similar stores in Kent.
English said: "We've had Ramsgate for about three years, Ashford just for just over a year and across the two shops in the last year alone we saw 55,500 transactions and we were able to save 170 tonnes of perfectly good food from going to waste, so they do work."
Some of the first to experienced the store were Shirley Graves and her partner Rod Taffs who have already filled their basket with bargains.
"People want to come down and see what they've got, it's amazing," says Graves.
"I've got a box of 20 samosas for Â£1.50 and a big huge bag of chicken for Â£6. Times are quite tight at the moment, being pensioners, it's cheap and the chicken is amazing."
"That's going to do us three or four meals," adds Taffs.
Medway Council leader, Vince Maple, said: "I think most people across Kent and Medway would want to see food not going to waste, so the ability to have good quality food at a reasonable price, helping not just our families and individuals on low incomes but helping all families has got to be a good thing."
The shop also has a confidential, soundproofed office pod at the back of the store where customers can seek personal advice and guidance.
The SEK Community Food Shop in The Pentagon Centre, Chatham, is open Monday to Saturday between 10:00 and 18:00.

items.body:
The Very Group teams with AI powered e-commerce personalisation firm Made With Intent
The Very Group, which operates digital retailers Very and Littlewoods, has partnered with Made With Intent. By using over 800 behavioural signals, Made With Intent’s agentic decision engine predicts customer’s intent in real-time, helping to decide what they see and when.
Very says it will now be able to spotlight discount offers unique to customers based on individual shopping trends, as well as provide prompts at crucial moments throughout the shopping experience. Made With Intent’s engine is built on a proprietary model and optimisation AI agent that work together to allocate experiences across hundreds of intent combinations, learning what works for which visitors and contexts then applying it to future sessions.
Sarah Hanna, Digital Director at The Very Group, comments: “Made With Intent’s agentic platform unlocks fast paced, scalable real-time personalisation that can be executed to help enhance the customer experience, ultimately influencing our commercial KPIs. In fact, in the first month of the partnership, we’ve already seen promising results including revenue per customer increasing by a fifth in one of our agentic strategies, and an uplift in overall conversion.”
“Made With Intent gives our e-commerce team a brand new lever that they can effortlessly activate to make a difference on what our customers see and when, whether that’s one-off discounts or personalised payment options. It’s all about giving customers the right experience at the right time.”
David Mannheim, Founder at Made With Intent, says: “Personalisation is a word you hear a lot when talking about retail, especially online. Our agentic AI decision engine gives innovative teams like Very’s the scale that’s needed to deliver more impactful, hyper-personalised customer experiences. Our goal has always been to move e-commerce away from generic, static experiences designed for everyone towards something more personalised and real-time. Not only because it is a better experience for visitors, but because it finds new growth, and we’re excited to be on this journey with The Very Group.”
So hot right now
Made With Intent is included in RTIH’s first ever Retail Technology Hot 100 List. Launching in August, this sees us bringing you the hottest companies whose solutions and systems are helping drive the retail sector forward.
Our Founder and Editor, Scott Thompson, drew up a list of 150 companies that had consistently been on his radar over the past 12 months whilst bringing our community the latest retail tech news and views that matter. These companies operate across the omnichannel retail landscape (stores, online, mobile, supply chain, payments etc).
Our judging panel, including Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO, Holland & Barrett, Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, Dr. Astha Purohit, Director of Product Management, Customer Data and Identity, Walmart, and Paula Bobbett, Chief Data and Digital Officer, Boots, provided feedback on those who have the most innovative, forward thinking technology offerings and are also best addressing retailers' current challenges, painpoints, and opportunities.
The judges used the following framework when making their picks:
1. Retailer problem fit - how meaningful, strategic, and widely felt the retailer pain being addressed is.
2. Production traction in retail (2025–2026) - real named retailer deployments, pilots. 
3. Innovation and defensibility - genuine technical novelty paired with a defensible competitive position.
And there was also a public vote, with thousands of members of our community of retail tech enthusiasts getting involved. Thanks to all those who took part! Based on the judging panel's feedback and the public vote, we then drew up our first ever RTIH Retail Technology Hot 100.
So, without further ado, here are the 100 hottest global retail technology ventures right now. Drum roll, please…

items.body:
Hamburg-based startup Procuros raises €20 million Series A for autonomous b2b trade push
Hamburg-based software company Procuros has announced the closing of a €20 million Series A funding round led by XAnge, with W23 Global joining as a new investor. This takes total funding to date to €34 million.
Existing backers Point Nine, Creandum, SquareOne and b2venture are joining again, alongside several angel investors. Procuros will use the cash to accelerate its AI native supply chain connectivity platform and expand its trading network internationally.
Over 300 companies are using Procuros, including Breuninger, Chefs Culinar, KoRo, flaconi, The Quality Group (ESN) and Hitschler, with more than €3 billion in annualised order volume said to be flowing through the platform.
“AI is advancing at incredible speed, while supply chains still run on infrastructure built decades ago. Operations teams are forced to bridge these gaps between systems that simply don’t communicate. We built Procuros to change that. Our infrastructure gives retailers, suppliers and AI agents the connectivity and trusted data they need to automate trade and make autonomous supply chains possible. Because ultimately, AI agents are only as good as the infrastructure they run on,” says Patrick Thelen, CEO and Co-Founder at Procuros (pictured below).
"Procuros is showing that AI agents can make autonomous B2B trade a reality today. The team has built the infrastructure AI agents need to work across entire tradingnetworks and proven the model at scale in DACH. What excites us is the opportunity ahead: to take this beyond its home market and establish an entirely new category for global B2B trade,” says Valerie Bures-Bönström, Partner and Managing Director DACH at XAnge.

AI will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.

items.body:
Cotswold Outdoor Group ramps up its retail media strategy to in-store with Broadsign and IUF partnership
Broadsign and IUF have announced a collaboration with UK retailer, Cotswold Outdoor Group, to expand its retail media network with an in-store advertising infrastructure. This, according to those involved, provides a unified workflow that streamlines media planning, management, and measurement in-store and across onsite and offsite channels.
The aim is to enable Cotswold’s brand partners to execute omnichannel ad campaigns that engage shoppers at the point of purchase and beyond. The network presently includes 149 till, shelf, totem, large format, and front-of-store displays across 23 stores, which are powered by the Broadsign platform (specifically the Broadsign CMS and Ad Server) and support a range of media.
The platform is helping to streamline operations and centralise content management and network health monitoring. The technology is also advancing screen monetisation opportunities by scheduling ads, automating yield, and balancing complex campaign rules to help Cotswold Outdoor Group capture optimal revenue. Through Broadsign’s integration with Zitcha, Cotswold Outdoor Group’s retail media platform, brand partners, and agencies can extend omnichannel strategies into the physical store environment.
“We’re passionate about helping people get closer to the outdoors, and that starts with creating inspiring moments. Our brand partners are a big part of that journey, and this collaboration with Broadsign and IUF offers a powerful new way to connect with our customers in-store, alongside our onsite and offsite media channels,” says Mary Antieul, Head of Commercial, Cotswold Outdoor Group.
“It means we can bring the right messages to shoppers at the right moment, with less friction for brands and a more connected experience for customers. The early results have been really encouraging, and we’re excited to build on that momentum as we expand the network and explore future programmatic opportunities.”
“Retail media is evolving fast, and partnering with IUF, we’ve delivered an in-store media infrastructure for Cotswold that can scale rapidly. Together, we’ve designed a network that makes it easy for its team to add, manage, control, and monetise new screens and integrate programmatic trading capabilities down the line,” says Frank Vallenga, Vice President, Platform Sales, EMEA and SEA at Broadsign. “By leveraging our integration with Zitcha, Cotswold has been able to connect audiences across their various retail media channels, which is a challenge many retailers have yet to solve.”
“This project went from tender to a live network generating revenue within 12 weeks which demonstrates the expertise of all of the technical partners involved,” says Josh Bunce, CEO at IUF. “Together we were able to deliver a cohesive customer journey so that Cotswold Outdoor Group can maximise its in-store retail proposition today but also ensure that it can scale easily into the future. The in-store channel is proving to be a competitive differentiator when advertisers start mapping out budgets with brands already seeing impressive results from the in-store activations.”

Morrisons talks embracing opportunities in data and AI as Mohsen Ghasempour joins grocery retailer
Rami Baitiéh, CEO at Morrisons, has taken to social media to discuss the appointment of Mohsen Ghasempour as Chief AI Officer, a newly created role that will see him establish a central data science and AI function for the UK grocery retailer. He joins from Kingfisher, where he had served as Chief AI Officer since March 2024 following more than two years as Group AI Director.
In a LinkedIn post, Baitiéh said: “To keep delivering exceptional value and service, we have to constantly innovate. That's why I am so excited to welcome Mohsen Ghasempour to Morrisons in the newly created role of Chief AI Officer. The creation of this new department reflects our commitment to ensuring we embrace the opportunities in data and AI at pace, with focus, and in the right way.”
He added: “Mohsen is a recognised expert in the field with hands on experience of unlocking the potential of technology to deliver innovative new solutions. Under his leadership, we will put that technology to work where it matters most: driving customer growth, pushing the boundaries of our manufacturing, operational, and commercial excellence, and genuinely empowering our colleagues to deliver measurable business impact.”
He concluded: “Mohsen brings a phenomenal track record, joining us from Kingfisher where he built and scaled their AI operations across Europe under the leadership of my friend, Thierry Garnier. I'm delighted to welcome him to Morrisons, and I'm so glad he could join us on our Leadership Meeting day. Mohsen, a warm welcome to the team!”
Kingfisher
Kingfisher Group, which owns B&Q and Screwfix in the UK and Castorama and Brico Depot in France and other markets, is using AI enabled productivity tools, including Fabric, to accelerate content creation, enhance SEO and improve conversion.
The FTSE 100 home improvement retailer lifted the lid last month on its AI and other tech initiatives as it raised its profit target despite seeing a heatwave driven drop off in sales at B&Q. It now expects to make a pre-tax profit of between £595 million and £635 million, having previously guided between £565 million and £625 million. Last year, it posted a £560 million profit.
Other highlights from its full year profit guidance and HY26/27 results include: group e-commerce sales reached 22% penetration. Group app sales now account for 29% of e-commerce sales, with app customers spending approximately 14% more than non-app users.
AI driven personalisation increased +16% generating approximately £100 million of sales, showing, Kingfisher claims, the growing value of its data and digital capabilities. Click & Collect sales were up +9% and home delivery sales +15%, supported by store-based fulfilment network and marketplace growth.
Screwfix Sprint (20 min delivery) was up +50% reflecting the growing demand for rapid fulfilment, particularly in Kingfisher’s City stores. Marketplace GMV rose +42% to £372 million, representing 18% of e-commerce sales. There has been investment in platform enhancements including Buybox, which helps customers find the best offer from multiple vendors by balancing price, merchant performance and delivery speed.
B&Q, meanwhile, continued to stump up cash for search and navigation capabilities, supporting improvements in online traffic and conversion. Natural language search is planned for implementation at B&Q in H2. The next phase of digital commerce will also include agent enabled shopping experiences.

items.body:
Shopify research: AI savvy UK shoppers set to spend £165 this Christmas but will make brands earn it
Consumers are entering the holiday season under significant economic pressure, with 53% of UK shoppers saying recent conditions have negatively affected their shopping plans. Planned Black Friday weekend spending across the UK is expected to drop to £165 on average from £181 in 2025.
A Shopify survey was conducted among 18,000 consumers in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Spain, the UK and the US. And also 7,500 owners and business decision-makers across Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Spain, the UK and the US in companies with fewer than 1,000 employees.
One third of British shoppers have postponed a purchase in the past year because of increased living costs. To combat this, they are value-maxxing: spending more time researching, comparing and weighing up whether a purchase is genuinely worth it. 86% of Brits feel more in control after researching. They’re also turning carts into watchlists. 28% said they deliberately leave products in their cart to see if the price drops. When shoppers did leave items in their carts, 32% said they return to complete the purchase when the price drops, while 29% buy after a discount code, voucher or special offer becomes available.
For today’s British consumers, value does not simply mean paying less. 54% define good value as receiving higher-than-expected quality for the price, while 38% say it means products having a longer lifespan than expected. A further 37% associate good value with earning bonus loyalty points.
UK businesses are hopeful, with 82% expecting higher sales over the holiday season this year (in line with sentiment in 2025), despite grappling with rising costs (45%), increased competition (38%) and disruption to supply chains (23%). In a season where every new sale will be hard won, they are looking beyond the immediate transaction and prioritising long-term loyalty. Returning-customer discounts (40%), loyalty or rewards programmes (38%), and improvements to delivery, tracking and returns (36%) are among the approaches businesses say are most effective at building longer-term relationships.
“UK consumers have not stopped spending, but every purchase now has to earn its place. With 53% saying recent economic conditions have affected their shopping plans, businesses cannot assume that a discount alone will secure the sale this holiday season. They need to show UK shoppers why their product is worth choosing, make the path to purchase as clear as possible and deliver an experience that gives customers a reason to come back,” says Stephen Rogan, Head of Customer Success, EMEA at Shopify.
As shoppers work harder to find the right product, AI is becoming part of the research process. Nearly two-thirds (64%) in the UK are likely to use AI for at least one shopping task during the holiday period, most commonly to find deals (29%) or discover products and inspiration (23%). Shoppers still draw a line at handing over the full purchase, though. Over half (52%) are comfortable letting AI recommend the right product, and 41% would let it build their cart, but only 28% trust it to complete a purchase on their behalf.
And businesses are preparing for AI assisted shopping: 45% are creating AI generated content, while a similar number (45%) are prioritising AI powered chatbots and virtual assistants. Meanwhile, 41% are making their stores easier for AI assistants to read and recommend. In addition to becoming a powerful filter for helping shoppers decide what is worth considering, AI is also creating opportunities for smaller brands to stand out more. 76% of UK shoppers who use AI most frequently are much more likely to choose independent or niche brands, compared with 45% of non users. Heavy users are also much less interested in buying from mass market brands than they were last year (59%) and are choosing more products that feel personal, intentional or considered (81%).
This creates a new opportunity for businesses that can clearly communicate what makes their product different. 47% of UK businesses are emphasising products that are unique or hard to find, while 38% are highlighting where and how their products are made, and the same (38%) are drawing attention to their independent or small-business status.
When thinking about what would make them reach for AI tools more, access to information makes the difference. 29% of British consumers said clear prices and discounts would make them more likely to use AI tools, while 27% noted the ability to compare products against similar options and a fifth said clear delivery times and shipping costs would increase the likelihood.
“AI is changing the front door to commerce for UK shoppers. They are using it to discover new products and brands, creating a powerful opportunity for independent and specialist businesses to be found. To best benefit, UK businesses need to ensure the fundamentals are in place, from accurate product information and inventory to clear pricing and delivery details, so both shoppers and their AI assistants can understand what makes their products worth choosing,” says Rogan.
“With 44% of consumers expecting to split their shopping evenly between online and offline this season, while 32% will shop mainly online and 17% mainly in-store, connected data for a seamless shopping experience will be critical. This holiday season, the brands that win will not necessarily offer the deepest discount. They’ll be the ones to make their products easy to discover, give shoppers clear proof of quality and value, and deliver an experience worth returning to.”
So hot right now
Shopify is included in RTIH’s first ever Retail Technology Hot 100 List. Launching in August, this sees us bringing you the hottest companies whose solutions and systems are helping drive the retail sector forward.
Our Founder and Editor, Scott Thompson, drew up a list of 150 companies that had consistently been on his radar over the past 12 months whilst bringing our community the latest retail tech news and views that matter. These companies operate across the omnichannel retail landscape (stores, online, mobile, supply chain, payments etc).
Our judging panel, including Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO, Holland & Barrett, Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, Dr. Astha Purohit, Director of Product Management, Customer Data and Identity, Walmart, and Paula Bobbett, Chief Data and Digital Officer, Boots, provided feedback on those who have the most innovative, forward thinking technology offerings and are also best addressing retailers' current challenges, painpoints, and opportunities.
The judges used the following framework when making their picks:
1. Retailer problem fit - how meaningful, strategic, and widely felt the retailer pain being addressed is.
2. Production traction in retail (2025–2026) - real named retailer deployments, pilots. 
3. Innovation and defensibility - genuine technical novelty paired with a defensible competitive position.
And there was also a public vote, with thousands of members of our community of retail tech enthusiasts getting involved. Thanks to all those who took part! Based on the judging panel's feedback and the public vote, we then drew up our first ever RTIH Retail Technology Hot 100.
So, without further ado, here are the 100 hottest global retail technology ventures right now. Drum roll, please…

Walmart and Wing are expanding their American drone delivery service to Seattle and Denver
Walmart and Wing have announced the next phase of their US wide network roll-out with plans to bring 30-minute drone delivery to Denver and Seattle metros in 2027, bringing home delivery of thousands of Walmart items to more than 20 major US metros.
To date, the tie up has brought drone delivery access to more than three million customers across major US metropolitan areas, including Dallas-Fort Worth, Atlanta, Houston and Orlando.
“Adding new metros to our expansion speaks to how quickly people across the country are adopting drone delivery," says Heather Rivera, Chief Business Officer at Wing. "We're excited to serve the needs of busy families in nearly 20 major markets spanning diverse communities and climates by delivering the everyday items these families need fast.”
“Expanding drone delivery to Seattle and Denver is about giving more customers a practical option when they need something quickly,” says Greg Cathey, Senior Vice President, eCommerce Transformation, Walmart. “Our stores put everyday items close to the communities we serve, and Wing helps bring those items to customers’ homes in minutes.”
Wing and Walmart are working toward reaching more than 270 total Walmart stores coast to coast. This will bring drone delivery to over 40 million customers across some of the largest metros in the nation, including Puget Sound.
“Innovation is a part of our way of life in Federal Way and around the Puget Sound. We look forward to Walmart and Wing’s drone delivery service bringing the region an incredible new convenience,” says Mayor of Federal Way Jim Ferrell. “By bringing advanced delivery solutions to our residents, we are supporting innovation, creating opportunities for future growth, and enhancing convenience for everyday things people need. The future has arrived and its being delivered by Walmart by drone.”
Cruising at speeds up to 60 mph, Wing’s aircraft can carry up to five pounds and deliver tens of thousands of Walmart items.

Snappy Shopper is included in RTIH’s first ever Retail Technology Hot 100 List. Launching in August, this sees us bringing you the hottest companies whose solutions and systems are helping drive the retail sector forward.
Our Founder and Editor, Scott Thompson, drew up a list of 150 companies that had consistently been on his radar over the past 12 months whilst bringing our community the latest retail tech news and views that matter. These companies operate across the omnichannel retail landscape (stores, online, mobile, supply chain, payments etc).
Our judging panel, including Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO, Holland & Barrett, Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, Dr. Astha Purohit, Director of Product Management, Customer Data and Identity, Walmart, and Paula Bobbett, Chief Data and Digital Officer, Boots, provided feedback on those who have the most innovative, forward thinking technology offerings and are also best addressing retailers' current challenges, painpoints, and opportunities.
The judges used the following framework when making their picks:
1. Retailer problem fit - how meaningful, strategic, and widely felt the retailer pain being addressed is.
2. Production traction in retail (2025–2026) - real named retailer deployments, pilots. 
3. Innovation and defensibility - genuine technical novelty paired with a defensible competitive position.
And there was also a public vote, with thousands of members of our community of retail tech enthusiasts getting involved. Thanks to all those who took part! Based on the judging panel's feedback and the public vote, we then drew up our first ever RTIH Retail Technology Hot 100.
So, without further ado, here are the 100 hottest global retail technology ventures right now. Drum roll, please…

items.body:
Relevance that can pass a security review: what tech and security leaders need to know about Rokt
For the engineers and security chiefs who keep e-commerce running, the mandate rarely changes. Support growth without making the stack harder to defend or harder to maintain. Real-time relevance, the AI driven practice of choosing the single most useful next action for a shopper, tests that mandate directly.
It sits next to checkout and payment, the systems technology teams guard most closely, and it depends on exactly the kind of data and decisioning that makes a chief information security officer ask hard questions.
Rokt, the New York-based e-commerce technology company, has begun making its case to those leaders directly. In a post addressed to technology and security leaders, part of a broader series on what it calls the transaction moment, the company argues that relevance can be delivered securely, reliably, and at scale without bolting new complexity onto the commerce stack. The claim is worth examining, in part because the timing makes it harder to meet.
Agentic commerce turns consent into an architecture problem
The complication is the arrival of AI agents that research, compare, and increasingly act on a customer's behalf. That forces a set of questions that used to be theoretical. How should a system tell human activity apart from agent-assisted and agent-initiated activity? How is a shopper's authority represented and passed along?
What context has to travel with an action for it to be accountable, and what records will a business need afterward to reconstruct what happened? Writing in Fast Company, Rokt chief commercial officer Elizabeth Buchanan argued that “the agent economy is no longer speculative; it's investable,” a shift that pushes these concerns out of strategy decks and into architecture diagrams.
The money behind the trend is now being modelled. A December 2025 eMarketer forecast cited in Rokt's own analysis of real-time relevance projects that AI platforms will drive $20.6 billion of US retail e-commerce sales in 2026 and $144 billion by 2029, while a broader Morgan Stanley estimate reaches $190 billion to $385 billion by 2030. Whatever the exact figure proves to be, the engineering implication is the same. The systems that handle consent, identity, and context at the transaction will carry more weight, not less.
The build trap
That is where the pitch meets a decision every technology leader recognises. Real-time relevance is not something a company builds once and leaves alone. It requires architecture, data pipelines, a decisioning layer, delivery, experimentation, governance, and continuous optimisation, each of which has to stay reliable as markets, rules, and use cases change. An internal build offers control, but the cost runs well past the first deployment and into years of maintenance.
Buying does not remove the diligence, the company acknowledges. It relocates it. Instead of estimating engineering hours, a CTO, chief architect, or head of platform operations ends up interrogating the vendor's architecture, security posture, reliability, data boundaries, and operating model, and asking whether all of it meets the standard the business would hold itself to. For data and AI teams, the added question is whether first-party data can be activated inside governed, measurable decisioning rather than shipped somewhere it can no longer be tracked.
What Rokt puts on the table
Rokt's technical answer centers on two components. The Rokt Brain is the decisioning engine that selects the next best action and native experience for each customer in real time. The Rokt Network supplies the reach and access to billions of e-commerce transaction moments that give the models something to learn from.
Per Rokt by the Numbers, the platform powers more than 13 billion transactions in 2026, the kind of volume a high traffic environment usually needs a partner to handle. The company recently shipped Brain V4, a new version of the engine built specifically for real-time e-commerce decisions, and it positions Rokt mParticle, its customer data platform with more than 300 native integrations, as the layer that unifies permitted first-party data behind those decisions.
The security posture
On the questions a security team asks first, Rokt leans on external certification. The platform supports enterprise grade certifications including SOC 2 and ISO 27001, and the company reports 99.992 percent uptime, a figure that speaks to the reliability half of technical trust. Certifications alone do not close an evaluation, as the company itself notes, since teams still have to judge how a platform manages access, monitoring, and change over time.
On data, Rokt describes itself as a trusted intermediary rather than an owner. The e-commerce business keeps ownership of its first-party data, customer experience, and customer relationship, and a client's data is used only for that client's purpose and is not shared with anyone else.
Proof by experiment
For technology and data teams, the most persuasive evidence tends to be operational rather than rhetorical. Rokt frames its relationships as continuous experiments, in which changes are tested on a slice of traffic, measured against clear outcomes, and scaled only when the numbers hold. Ankit Dutta, data science lead for commerce at Block, described that rhythm in the company's Afterpay partnership, saying “every interaction generates data, and every data point informs our next optimisation.”
Outside the case studies, Rokt's profile has been climbing. The deal tracking service Dealroom noted revenue above $800 million in 2025. The company appeared for the first time in the 2026 Gartner Market Guide for Retail and Commerce Media Networks and was shortlisted for the AdExchanger 2026 AI Innovator award, and a trade analysis of the sector's next phase credited its decisioning approach as a reason it has pulled ahead. For a technology or security leader, none of that is proof of fit, but it is the kind of signal that makes a closer evaluation worthwhile.
The argument Rokt makes to engineering and security leaders is narrower than the one it makes to marketers. It is not that relevance drives revenue, though the company says it does. It is that relevance only becomes a durable enterprise capability when it can operate inside the controls a business already trusts. Judged that way, the decision facing a CTO or CISO is less about whether real-time relevance is valuable and more about whether it can be run without widening the surface they are paid to protect.

items.title: Sainsbury’s and Morrisons ‘held talks this year’ on multibillion-pound merger
items.summary: Deal would have created a supermarket with a market share of 23.6%, still well behind Tesco’s 27.8% Sainsbury’s held merger talks with rival Morrisons this year to discuss a multibillion-pound deal that would have been the biggest shake-up for UK supermarkets in decades, according to reports. The two companies held exploratory negotiations, according to the Financial Times and Sky. It is believed they are no longer in live discussions. Continue reading...
items.body:
Sainsbury’s held merger talks with rival Morrisons this year to discuss a multibillion-pound deal that would have been the biggest shake-up for UK supermarkets in decades, according to reports.
The two companies held exploratory negotiations, according to the Financial Times and Sky. It is believed they are no longer in live discussions.
Morrisons, which was once one of the big four UK grocers alongside Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Asda, was bought by the US private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice in 2021.
The deal loaded it with more than £7bn in debt on its balance sheet, and it has since struggled to grow as fast as its rivals. The German discounter Lidl overtook it in market share this year.
A merger between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would have created a business with a 23.6% market share, putting it still some way behind Britain’s biggest retailer, Tesco, which has 27.8% of the market, according to analysts at Worldpanel by Numerator.
The last attempt to merge two of the big four supermarkets was in 2019, when Asda and Sainsbury’s almost joined forces. That £7bn deal was blocked by the Competition and Markets Authority on the basis that it would result in a loss of competition and higher prices for customers.
The CMA would have almost certainly reviewed any merger between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons, and could have required the former to sell some of its stores to gain approval for any deal.
Reducing competition in the grocery sector could also be politically sensitive, given that millions of households have grappled with persistent food inflation in recent years.
Clayton Dubilier & Rice, however, is open to a tie-up between Morrisons and another major supermarket, according to Sky. It reported that Asda, which is majority owned by the private equity firm TDR Capital, could also be drawn into deal talks.
Shares in Sainsbury’s, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, were flat on Monday afternoon. The stock has fallen by 3% so far this year, compared with a 6% rise for its FTSE 100 rival Tesco.
Sainsbury’s, which employs about 140,000 people, is the second biggest grocer in the UK by market share at 15.2%.
It agreed to sell Argos for £120m in the summer to allow it to concentrate on its core food business, a decade after buying the retail chain for more than £1bn.
News of supermarket takeover talks came as Lidl GB reported a 10% jump in its annual revenue to more than £13bn on Monday.
The company said pre-tax profits at its British arm rose by 30% to £245.5m in the year that ended in February as shoppers sought out cheaper fresh meat, fruit and vegetables, as well as its Deluxe upmarket food range.
Sainsbury’s and Morrisons declined to comment.

items.title: Sainsbury's and Argos to hire 17,500 Christmas temps... and you get up to 15% staff discount
items.summary: The positions, which pay up to £16 per hour, will be scattered across supermarkets, stores and warehouses, as well as delivery driver roles.
items.body:
Sainsbury's and Argos to hire 17,500 Christmas temps... and you get up to 15% staff discount
Sainsbury's and Argos are offering 17,500 temporary Christmas roles across Britain.
The positions, which pay up to £16 per hour, will be scattered across Sainsbury’s supermarkets, convenience stores, warehouses, Argos stores and online fulfilment operations.
For in-store jobs you can earn between £13.23 and £14.54 per hour, while delivery driver roles pay slightly more.
As an Argos driver you can earn £14.23 to £15.54 per hour, and as a Sainsbury's driver, you can earn between £14.73 to £16.04 per hour.
Pay varies by role and location to reflect the different responsibilities involved and local market conditions.
Job opportunities: Sainsbury's and Argos will hire 17,500 Christmas temps this year
One major perk of the job is that seasonal staff receive an uncapped colleague discount of 10 per cent at Sainsbury's and Argos.
This will rise to 15 per cent off every Friday and Saturday if you work at Sainsbury's.
Seasonal staff at the supermarket also receive free food during shifts.
Christmas temps will be employed on fixed-term contracts ranging from four to 12 weeks.
For most roles, you must be over 18 years old. You must also have Right to Work eligibility in the UK.
Delivery drivers must have a full UK drivers licence that has been valid for the past 12 months.
Motorists will have to complete an online driving risk assessment as part of their interview
For both roles you might have to carry heavy loads. For example, delivery drivers must be able to move containers weighing up to 15kg.
And when you're not out making deliveries you might have to help across the store as needed.
If you'd like to apply, visit the Sainsbury's Christmas Job Opportunities or speak to your local store.
Tracey Clements, chief retail, logistics and supply chain officer at Sainsbury’s, said: 'Christmas is always a special time for our customers and colleagues and our seasonal team members help make it happen.
'We look forward to welcoming thousands of new colleagues who will help us deliver great-tasting festive food, brilliant service and fantastic value across our stores, fulfilment centres and delivery operations.
'Whether someone is joining us for the first time or returning for another Christmas, they’ll play an important role in helping customers celebrate.'
Sainsbury's agreed to sell the Argos business to Swift Partners earlier this year but the deal has not yet completed.

items.summary: A merger between the two would be one of the biggest supermarket deals in more than five years and create a giant with a market share of 23.6 per cent.
items.body:
Sainsbury's held blockbuster merger talks with rival Morrisons
Sainsbury's held talks with smaller rival Morrisons over a potential merger before walking away earlier this year.
Sainsbury's reportedly held discussions with the private-equity-owned Morrisons between November 2025 and February of this year. The two supermarkets are no longer in active talks, the Financial Times reported.
A merger between the two would be one of the biggest supermarket deals in more than five years and create a giant with a market share of 23.6 per cent.
Britain’s number one supermarket Tesco holds 27.8 per cent of the grocery market, according to industry researchers Worldpanel.
A blockbuster deal would have come under fierce scrutiny from the competition watchdog, and Sainsbury's would have had to sell some of its shops to get the green light.
A merger between Sainsbury's and Morrisons would create a larger rival to market leader Tesco
Sainsbury’s attempt to buy Asda, the third-biggest grocer, in a £7.3billion takeover swoop was thwarted by the Competition and Markets Authority in 2019. They argued it would limit competition and discourage supermarkets from keeping prices low for customers.
Morrisons' owner, the private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice, remains open to a deal with a major rival, according to a Sky News report.
The grocer has been struggling to retain customers since its debt-fuelled £10billion takeover in 2021.
German discounters Aldi and Lidl have also posed a major threat to the traditional supermarket heavyweights, snapping up market share over the last fifteen years.
Aldi and Lidl's growing prominence - holding a combined total of just under 20 per cent of the market - could increase the likelihood of regulators giving Sainsbury's and Morrisons a green light, should they revive any discussions.
The reports come just a couple of months after Sainsbury’s agreed to sell its general merchandise business Argos to a new firm Swift Partners for £120million. It had originally bought it in a deal worth £1.4 billion in 2016.
Sainsbury's has been battling discounters through a focus on the food side of its business, appealing to customers with lower prices through its Nectar loyalty scheme and alternatives to dining out.
Sainsbury’s and Morrisons did not want to comment.

items.title: Jeremy Clarkson at Tory conference: ‘Why would anybody set up a business in this country?’
items.summary: Jeremy Clarkson hit out at the Labour government over its decision in 2024 to impose higher inheritance taxes on farming land two days before Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to call for a cut.  Clarkson said government officials failed to understand the impact of changes facing family farms as some owners had to sell [...]
items.body:
Jeremy Clarkson at Tory conference: ‘Why would anybody set up a business in this country?’
Jeremy Clarkson hit out at the Labour government over its decision in 2024 to impose higher inheritance taxes on farming land two days before Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to call for a cut.
Clarkson said government officials failed to understand the impact of changes facing family farms as some owners had to sell land.
Speaking on stage at the Conservative Party conference, the Diddly Squat farm owner said a decision to cap the 100 per cent agricultural property relief for inheritance tax at land and business assets totalling £1m. A government U-turn in late 2025 then led Labour ministers to raise the threshold to £2.5m.
“I think they didn’t understand it when they introduced it,” Clarkson said. “With a farm it’s completely different because you’d have to sell a bit of it, making it even less profitable, or you’d sell the whole lot.”
“It makes perfect sense for the way the countryside looks and our food supply system for farmers to pass it on to the only people who know how to do it, which is your kids.”
Reflecting on the challenges facing the farming sector, the former Top Gear start said: “Not every farmer has a quiz show to host on ITV, I think that’s the essence of it. If you’re an ordinary farmer, this is not just the weather, the attacks come from everywhere.”
Clarkson also revealed his “dream” of opening another pub outside the UK. “Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?” he asked on stage, adding: “I’ll see if I can do it abroad somewhere. I probably won’t, but I’m dreaming of it.”
His intervention comes ahead of the leader’s speech on Wednesday where Badenoch is expected to state her intention to cut inheritance taxes.
On the weekend, the Tory leader said inheritance taxes were “immoral”.
Badenoch’s possible tax announcement
The expected announcement, first reported in The Mail On Sunday and followed up elsewhere, could be a flagship announcement in Wednesday’s speech.
Inheritance tax of 40 per cent is levied on all estates with property worth more than £500,000. A couple can combine their allowances to pass on up to £1 million to their children.
The thresholds have been frozen for several years, dragging several more families into tax bands.
The Tories have so far announced spending cuts across welfare, aid and other areas worth more than £47bn. The party has allocated about half of the savings on tax cuts and the other half towards paying down the level of government debt.
Top shadow frontbenchers have insisted that the government would not make tax cuts until savings have been identified.
A party spokesman said rumours around an inheritance tax cut was “pure speculation”.
During his interview with the shadow environment secretary Victoria Atkins, Clarkson also said regulations on farmers had cost businesses.
“I think if there were far fewer rules and regulations, yes there would be bad apples, there would be farmers I’m sure of it who would use DDT [a synthetic insecticide] or whatever, quietly do things which were reprehensible,” Clarkson said.
“But the vast majority, I don’t think they would. The farmers I know – they want to protect their farms because they want to hand them onto their children.”

items.title: Sainsbury’s and Morrisons held talks over blockbuster merger
items.summary: Sainsbury’s walked away from talks over a merger with smaller rival Morrisons earlier this year, shelving what would have been the biggest shake-up of the UK’s grocery market in decades.  The UK’s second-largest supermarket chain held preliminary talks with its private-equity-owned rival over a merger of the two firms between November 2025 and February this [...]
items.body:
Sainsbury’s and Morrisons held talks over blockbuster merger
Sainsbury’s walked away from talks over a merger with smaller rival Morrisons earlier this year, shelving what would have been the biggest shake-up of the UK’s grocery market in decades.
The UK’s second-largest supermarket chain held preliminary talks with its private-equity-owned rival over a merger of the two firms between November 2025 and February this year, it is understood.
There are no active talks between the two sides but the two parties have not ruled out the possibility of discussions restarting in the future.
Sainsbury’s attempted to buy discount grocer Asda for £7.3bn in 2019, but had this deal blocked by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) on the grounds it would reduce competition and push up prices for shoppers.
A deal to combine Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would inevitably draw the scrutiny of the CMA, which could force the firm to sell stores to soothe fears of lessened competition.
Sainsbury’s holds a 15.2 per cent share of the UK’s grocery market, while Morrisons has a 8.4 per cent share, according to Worldpanel by Numerator.
A combination of the two grocers would take their presence in the market to 23.6 per cent, widening the gap on Asda and Aldi but still below Tesco’s 27.8 per cent. Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons were first reported by Sky News’ Mark Kleinman.
Morrisons creaks under debt pile
Sainsbury’s chief executive Simon Roberts has pushed the supermarket chain to focus on its food sales, which jumped by three per cent to £8bn in the three months to June.
In July, the group sold Argos to Swift Partners for £120m, after buying the catalogue retailer for £1.4bn a decade ago.
Morrisons, the UK’s sixth-largest supermarket chain, has been weighed down by a huge debt pile since its takeover by the New-York based Clayton Dubilier & Rice in 2021.
The group’s net debt grew from £7.1bn to £7.5bn in the year to October 2025 but the grocer last month posted sales growth for the fifteenth consecutive quarter.
Rami Batiéh, who joined Morrisons in 2023, said his turnaround of the grocer is delivering a “broad-based improvement” across the group as he battles to cut costs and keep prices down.
Sainsbury’s operates more than 600 supermarkets and nearly 900 convenience stores. Morrisons runs about 500 supermarkets and more than 1,700 convenience outlets.
Shares in Sainsbury’s fell on news of the collapsed talks, to a loss of about 0.3 per cent at 322p.
Morrisons and Sainsbury’s declined to comment.

items.title: Greens pitch Zohran Mamdani-style $25.1bn plan to nationalise 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets
items.summary: Former MP and Greens Institute head, Max Chandler-Mather, says proposal for publicly owned supermarket chain will ease grocery prices Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast More than 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets would be nationalised, and hundreds of government grocery stores opened, under a $25bn plan being put forward by former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather. Channelling New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan for publicly owned grocery stores, Chandler-Mather, the boss of the party’s thinktank, the Greens Institute, wants to use new forced divestiture laws to take over major supermarket sites and three distribution centres. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Continue reading...
items.body:
More than 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets would be nationalised, and hundreds of government grocery stores opened, under a $25bn plan being put forward by former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather.
Channelling New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan for publicly owned grocery stores, Chandler-Mather, the boss of the party’s thinktank, the Greens Institute, wants to use new forced divestiture laws to take over major supermarket sites and three distribution centres.
The government would fund another 424 new supermarkets and 10 distribution centres, taking about 20% of the market share of commercial operators for the new non-profit network.
Chandler-Mather says the new stores – dubbed Fair Go Grocers – would save consumers as much as 22% on the average shop, or $60 per week for a four-person household. Heavy discounts would be put in place for essentials including fruit and vegetables, bread, milk and meat.
A statutory authority would be established to set prices each month, as well as minimum wholesale rates for suppliers. Its members would include experts in supermarket operations, nutrition and food science, and farming.
The federal government would pay for capital costs including land, construction, and acquisition, and stores would be located in areas of the highest need.
After an initial $25.1bn price tag over five years, Chandler-Mather says the stores would be self-funded and not require additional taxpayer cash.
By comparison, the federal government currently spends about $24bn each year on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.
“Kids are going to school hungry, families are skipping meals, people are cutting back on essentials, all because Labor has allowed Coles and Woolworths to jack up prices for extra profit, regardless of the human consequences,” Chandler-Mather said.
“Just like healthcare and education, food is essential to life. And just like Medicare and public schools, it’s time we had a public option for food.”
The proposal is similar to Mamdani’s plan for five city-owned and subsidised grocery stores, one in each of New York City’s boroughs, opening by 2029. Last month a local business group sued the Democratic Socialist mayor, arguing existing small grocery stores would be unable to compete.
The New Zealand Greens have a plan to nationalise 120 supermarkets and establish a new publicly owned chain called KiwiMark.
The Greens Institute commissioned pollsters YouGov to test public support for the proposal last month, with background on Mamdani’s plan for government-owned stores that cut out profits made by private corporations.
Voters were asked: Would you support or oppose publicly owned supermarkets being tried in Australia? A total of 84% said they strongly supported or somewhat supported the idea, while 16% somewhat or strongly opposed the idea.
Support was strongest among voters aged 25-34 (88%), among Greens voters (96%) and women (88%).
Newly elected Greens leader David Shoebridge, under pressure to spur enthusiasm and attention for the party, has welcomed the proposal, saying the Greens should be focused on improving the material conditions of individuals, the environment and community.
“A publicly owned supermarket with cheaper food is wildly popular, because it makes people’s lives better,” he told Guardian Australia.
“Of course this is the sort of policy that we should be discussing right now.”
Shoebridge said Mamdani’s message about the government needing to address the needs of citizens was working.
“When I talk to people, I hear about the dread they feel heading down the supermarket aisle, the shopping trolley feels like pushing a boulder up to the checkout,” he said.
“While 99% of us are paying more for food, and many are making decisions about enough food or some other essentials, the 1% who own Coles and Woolies are laughing.”
The competition watchdog has brought cases against both Coles and Woolworths over false or misleading representations about in-store discounts, and a report released last year found they were among the most profitable grocers in the world.
The Greens allege Labor’s new laws banning supermarkets from excessive pricing are ineffective and have not resulted in lower costs for consumers.

items.title: Frasers to convert Harvey Nichols Bristol and Leeds sites to Flannels
items.summary: Frasers cief executive Michael Murray, son-in-law of Mike Ashley, said he hopes to 'invest significant sums of money' in the famous Harvey Nichols store in Knightsbridge.
items.body:
Frasers to convert Harvey Nichols Bristol and Leeds sites to Flannels
The boss of Frasers has promised to bring Harvey Nichols’ London store ‘back to its former glory’ but will convert the Bristol and Leeds sites to Flannels stores.
Michael Murray, whose father-in-law billionaire Mike Ashley owns Frasers, said he hopes to ‘invest significant sums of money’ in the famous Harvey Nichols store in Knightsbridge.
Frasers launched its £40million rescue deal to buy the luxury department store chain after the chain warned it would run out of money if it failed to secure new investment.
The company, which also owns Sports Direct, has been focusing more on the luxury market in recent years, including taking stakes in fashion labels Burberry and Mulberry.
As part of the deal, Murray said Harvey Nichols' Bristol and Leeds stores will become Flannels, the luxury retailer owned by Frasers, with plans to refurbish the Edinburgh and Manchester shops. Harvey Nichols in Birmingham will shut.
Murray told Vogue Business: ‘For the London store, we are in talks with the Cadogan estate who own the freehold of Knightsbridge because we’re prepared to invest significant sums of money in that building as long as we can get the right terms with the landlord.
Frasers, which also owns Sports Direct, is putting more cash into its luxury brands - including buying the Harvey Nichols department store chain
'We want to do something truly remarkable in London and bring it back to its former glory.’
‘The [conversion] of the Bristol and Leeds Harvey Nichols stores to Flannels is part of the broader luxury strategy, allowing us to retain a presence in these locations while aligning them with the Flannels proposition,’ Murray said in an interview with Vogue Business.
In its 1990s heyday, fans of the London shop included Princess Diana and other fashion-forward 'Sloane Rangers'.
Mary Portas, the store's young creative director, made a deal with Absolutely Fabulous where its brash and boozy fashionista characters often mentioned the store and wore its clothes.
She transformed it into a trendy destination for the 'fashion-forward' with eye-catching window displays.
But it has failed to make a profit for five years after being hit by a downturn in tourism spending following the Covid pandemic and the removal of a VAT-free shopping scheme.
Earlier this year, PR guru Lynne Franks, who worked for Harvey Nicks in its heyday and inspired Jennifer Saunders’ character Eddy in Ab Fab, told This is Money the business should try to revive its ‘uniquely creative’ history.
She added: ‘The flagship has got to improve and become more unique with brands and marketing - it needs to get exciting. Make it fun, make people want to go there as a destination. Let’s see what happens.’
Murray said Harvey Nicks was an appealing acquisition ‘because it is very different from Flannels,’ and appealed to women predominately. ‘It works with a large array of brands beyond the major luxury brands, and has 200 years of heritage, which means it has value internationally,’ he said.
He pointed to existing Harvey Nichols shops in Riyadh, Dubai, Doha and Kuwait and said he was ‘looking at expansion opportunities through franchise partners,’ as well as ‘opportunities’ in Georgia and India to open ‘big’ shops with partners.
Murray also addressed anxiety over the acquisition following its brief takeover of online luxury marketplace Matchesfashion. Just three months after buying Matchesfashion in December 2023 for £52million, Frasers placed the company into administration with 273 job losses. This led to designer brands, including the likes of Burberry and Gucci, being owed a total of £36million.
He said: ‘The main difference is that Harvey Nichols is a physical retail business. Matches’s business model was very difficult. Free postage, free returns, low margin, huge overheads. 'When you cut it all back, there was not a lot there.’

items.title: Lidl's UK boss calls for planning reform as discounter eyes 50 new stores this year
items.summary: The British arm of the German discount giant has been opening new shops as it seeks to grow an even greater slice of the market. It has been using price cuts and loyalty offers to win share.
items.body:
Lidl's UK boss calls for planning reform as discounter eyes 50 new stores this year
The boss of Lidl UK has warned that planning delays are hitting investment and costing jobs as it outlines plans to open 50 new stores.
Chief executive Ryan McDonnell called for a shake-up ‘that creates a faster, more efficient planning process’ as he revealed the grocer’s UK sales hit £13billion.
The British arm of the German discount giant, which recently overtook Morrisons to become the country's fifth-largest grocer, is seeking to grow its market share further with a £600million investment into new shops.
The company has also been trying to win more customers by price cuts and promotions, including through its Lidl Plus loyalty app.
It said revenue rose 10.8 per cent to £13billion over the year to February 28, 2026 – thanks to 40 new shops which opened during the period. Operating profits rose 9.9 per cent to £345million.
It said it won 43 million new shoppers and continued to be the UK’s ‘fastest-growing bricks-and-mortar supermarket.’
Lidl sold 486 million more products, with growth across fresh meat and fruit and vegetables, and said it invested a total of £315million into affordable prices.
Grocery price wars: German discounter Lidl has been poaching customers from other supermarkets
It comes as traditional supermarkets have been on the defensive and launched their own slew of price cuts over the past two years.
Sales have benefited from a shift that has seen Brits opt to ‘dine in’ rather than eating out at pubs and restaurants amid high living costs.
Lidl’s ‘premium deluxe’ range rose 12 per cent as McDonnell said ‘customers are increasingly looking to trade up and treat themselves at home.’
Boss McDonnell said there were ‘hundreds more opportunities for stores’ as the group looks to expand its footprint in key cities such as London and Glasgow.
But he added: ‘Any planning delays or administrative bottlenecks can of course slow down crucial investments, job creation, and local economic growth.
‘We would welcome reform that creates a faster, more efficient planning process.’
His remarks echo those of Next boss Lord Wolfson, who argued that the planning system is a larger hurdle for economic growth than business rates.
It is not the first time Lidl has railed against delays at local authorities leading to protracted planning processes.
Earlier this year, Richard Taylor, Lidl’s UK chief real estate officer, said the UK was ‘stuck in the slow lane’ and a ‘lack of consistency’ across planning authorities had delayed store openings.
McDonnell’s comments come a couple of months after the competition watchdog said that Aldi and Lidl should not be able to block rival supermarkets from opening close to their shops. They are set to be included with other large supermarkets - after an explosion in growth over the last decade.
McDonnell said the group ‘embrace that fair market competition’ and said he was not concerned that the changes would ‘slow our momentum as we continue expanding the store network.’
The business is ‘gearing up’ for ‘our biggest Christmas yet,’ he said.
McDonnell added: ‘Our performance is a clear testament to the trust that millions of customers place in us every week as a direct result of the dedication of our colleagues right across the country.
‘As we grow, our focus doesn't shift - we're constantly investing in low prices, high quality, and maximum value for our customers.’
Only Ocado, which sells groceries online, has been achieving better growth in recent months, according to industry researchers at Worldpanel.
Lidl overtook Morrisons as the country’s fifth biggest grocer in May.
Market researchers at Worldpanel said that Lidl held 8.7 per cent of the market over the three months to September 6, from 8.3 per cent a year ago
Its sales rose 8 per cent to £3.16billion over the period – eclipsing sales growth at rival Aldi, where sales grew just 0.7 per cent in the same period.
Lidl has had an impressive ascent, as 20 years ago it made up just 1.4 per cent of the market.

items.body:
The Very Group, which operates digital retailers Very and Littlewoods, has partnered with Made With Intent to enhance the digital shopping journey.
The new partnership will see Very offer its customers a more personalised experience than ever before. By using over 800 behavioural signals, Made With Intent’s agentic decision engine predicts customer’s intent in real-time, helping to decide what they see and when.
All based on customer behaviour and intention, Very will now be able to spotlight discount offers unique to customers based on individual shopping trends, as well as provide prompts at crucial moments throughout the shopping experience.
Made With Intent’s engine is built on a proprietary model and optimisation AI agent that work together to allocate experiences across hundreds of intent combinations, learning what works for which visitors and contexts then applying it to future sessions.
Sarah Hanna, digital director at The Very Group, commented: “Made With Intent’s agentic platform unlocks fast paced, scalable real-time personalisation that can be executed to help enhance the customer experience, ultimately influencing our commercial KPIs. In fact, in the first month of the partnership, we’ve already seen promising results including revenue per customer increasing by a fifth in one of our agentic strategies, and an uplift in overall conversion.
“Made With Intent gives our ecommerce team a brand-new lever that they can effortlessly activate to make a difference on what our customers see and when – whether that’s one-off discounts or personalised payment options. It’s all about giving customers the right experience at the right time.”
David Mannheim, founder of Made With Intent, added: “Personalisation is a word you hear a lot when talking about retail, especially online. Our agentic AI decision engine gives innovative teams like Very’s the scale that’s needed to deliver more impactful, hyper-personalised customer experiences. Our goal has always been to move ecommerce away from generic, static experiences designed for everyone towards something more personalised and real-time. Not only because it is a better experience for visitors, but because it finds new growth, and we’re excited to be on this journey with The Very Group.”
